questions.question: The Society of Actuaries (SOA) was formed in 1949 by merging which two organisations?

options.a: The Casualty Actuarial Society and the American Academy of Actuaries
options.b: The Institute of Actuaries and the Faculty of Actuaries
options.c: The Actuarial Society of America and the American Institute of Actuaries
options.d: The Actuarial Society of America and the Casualty Actuarial Society

questions.explanation: The SOA came from the 1949 merger of the Actuarial Society of America (founded 1889) and the American Institute of Actuaries (founded 1909). Option B describes the UK merger of 2010, and the CAS in A and D still exists as a separate body.

questions.topic: History and Professional Structure of Actuarial Science
questions.question: The Casualty Actuarial Society was founded in November 1914 under a different name and took its present name in 1921. What was its original name?

options.a: The Casualty Actuarial and Statistical Society of America

questions.explanation: The CAS began in 1914 as the Casualty Actuarial and Statistical Society and shortened its name in 1921. Options C and B are the two bodies that merged into the SOA in 1949, and D is not a real historical body.

questions.topic: History and Professional Structure of Actuarial Science
questions.question: When the Casualty Actuarial Society was founded in 1914, it was mainly concerned with which newly introduced line of insurance in the United States?
questions.explanation: The CAS was set up chiefly to handle the actuarial problems of workers' compensation, which had just been introduced in the US in the early 20th century. Life assurance (D), pensions (B) and health cover (A) are mainly SOA areas rather than casualty lines.

questions.topic: History and Professional Structure of Actuarial Science
questions.question: The Casualty Actuarial Society qualifies actuaries for one main practice area. Which of the following is NOT a CAS practice area?
questions.explanation: The CAS covers general insurance, also called property and casualty (P&C), such as motor, property and liability business; it does not qualify actuaries in life, pensions or health. Options A, D and B are all P&C work and so fall within the CAS's area.

questions.topic: History and Professional Structure of Actuarial Science
questions.question: Chinedu, a general insurance actuary in Lagos, completes the Associate requirements of the Casualty Actuarial Society. Which letters may he now use after his name?
questions.explanation: An Associate of the Casualty Actuarial Society uses ACAS; the Fellow designation FCAS (D) needs further exams after associateship. ASA (B) is the Society of Actuaries' associate title and AIA (A) was the old Institute of Actuaries' associate title.

questions.topic: History and Professional Structure of Actuarial Science
questions.question: The International Actuarial Association traces its origin to a committee set up in 1895 to organise international meetings of actuaries. Where was the first International Congress of Actuaries held that year?
questions.explanation: The first International Congress of Actuaries met in Brussels in 1895, and the permanent committee formed then (the Comite Permanent des Congres d'Actuaires) later became the IAA. Ottawa (A) is where the IAA is now headquartered, while London (C) and Edinburgh (D) are home to the IFoA's offices.

questions.topic: History and Professional Structure of Actuarial Science
questions.question: Following its 1998 restructuring at the International Congress in Birmingham, who are the full members of the International Actuarial Association?

options.b: Government insurance regulators of each country
options.c: National actuarial associations, so it is an association of associations
options.d: Individual actuaries who have passed its own examinations

questions.explanation: Since 1998 the IAA has been an association of national actuarial associations; individual actuaries take part through their national bodies and IAA sections. It sets no qualifying examinations of its own (D), and insurers (A) and regulators (B) are not its members.

questions.topic: History and Professional Structure of Actuarial Science
questions.question: The International Actuarial Association publishes International Standards of Actuarial Practice (ISAPs). How are these standards described?

options.a: Model standards that member associations are encouraged to align their own standards with
options.b: Accounting standards that insurers must use in their financial statements
options.c: Binding rules that every actuary in the world must follow
options.d: Examination syllabuses that replace national qualifications

questions.explanation: ISAPs are model standards of practice: they are not binding on any actuary, but national associations are encouraged to set standards that closely match them. Option C overstates their force, D confuses standards with exams, and B describes accounting standards such as IFRS.

questions.topic: History and Professional Structure of Actuarial Science
questions.question: Which actuarial body, with offices in Cape Town, offers actuarial qualifications for South Africa?

options.a: The Actuarial Society of South Africa (ASSA)

questions.explanation: ASSA is the South African actuarial society, based in Cape Town, and covers life, pensions, health and general insurance. The CAS (D) is based in Arlington, Virginia, NAS (B) is the Nigerian body, and the SOA (C) is based in the Chicago area.

questions.topic: History and Professional Structure of Actuarial Science
questions.question: Which of the following is the professional body for actuaries in Nigeria?

options.c: The Chartered Insurance Institute of Nigeria (CIIN)

questions.explanation: The Nigerian Actuarial Society is the professional association of actuaries and actuarial students practising in Nigeria. NAICOM (D) and PenCom (A) are government regulators of insurance and pensions, and the CIIN (C) is the professional body for insurance practitioners in general.

questions.topic: History and Professional Structure of Actuarial Science
questions.question: Which Nigerian government agency, established under an Act of 1997, regulates and supervises the insurance industry?
questions.explanation: NAICOM was established by the National Insurance Commission Act 1997 to regulate insurance business and protect policyholders. PenCom (C) regulates pensions, NAS (B) is a professional association rather than a regulator, and the SEC (D) regulates the capital market.

questions.topic: History and Professional Structure of Actuarial Science
questions.question: The National Pension Commission (PenCom), which regulates and supervises Nigeria's pension system, was established by which law?

options.c: The Companies and Allied Matters Act

questions.explanation: PenCom was created by the Pension Reform Act 2004 to regulate and supervise pensions and license pension fund administrators and custodians. The 1997 Act in option B created NAICOM, C governs company registration, and D is an old British law, not a Nigerian pension statute.

questions.topic: History and Professional Structure of Actuarial Science
questions.question: In January 2024, the University of Lagos obtained accreditation for its MSc Actuarial Science programme, earning graduates exam exemptions. Which body granted the accreditation?

options.d: The Institute and Faculty of Actuaries (IFoA)

questions.explanation: The IFoA accredited UNILAG's postgraduate MSc in Actuarial Science, giving successful graduates exam exemptions; the programme was developed with the Nigerian Actuarial Society. The SOA (B) and CAS (A) are North American bodies, and NAICOM (C) regulates insurers rather than accrediting degrees.

questions.topic: History and Professional Structure of Actuarial Science
questions.question: Which of the following correctly matches each Nigerian body with its main role?

options.a: NAICOM - professional body of actuaries; PenCom - regulates insurers; NAS - regulates pensions
options.b: NAICOM - regulates insurers; PenCom - regulates pensions; NAS - professional body of actuaries
options.c: NAICOM - regulates pensions; PenCom - regulates insurers; NAS - professional body of actuaries
options.d: NAICOM - regulates insurers; PenCom - professional body of actuaries; NAS - regulates pensions

questions.explanation: NAICOM supervises the insurance industry, PenCom supervises pensions, and the Nigerian Actuarial Society represents the actuarial profession. Option C swaps the two regulators, while A and D wrongly turn a regulator into a professional body.

questions.topic: History and Professional Structure of Actuarial Science
questions.question: Under the IFoA qualification pathway, what must a student complete to become an Associate?

options.a: The Core Principles exams only, with no work experience requirement
options.b: Two Specialist Principles exams and one Specialist Advanced exam
options.c: All exams including Specialist Advanced, plus 3 years of PPD
options.d: The Core Principles and Core Practices exams, 2 years of PPD and Professional Skills Stages 1 and 2

questions.explanation: IFoA associateship comes after the Core Principles (CS, CM, CB) and Core Practices (CP) exams together with 2 years of Personal and Professional Development and Professional Skills Stages 1 and 2. Option A leaves out the practice exams and experience, while B and C describe the further steps needed for fellowship.

questions.topic: History and Professional Structure of Actuarial Science
questions.question: After becoming an IFoA Associate, what further requirements lead to Fellowship?

options.a: Two Specialist Principles exams, one Specialist Advanced exam and a total of 3 years of PPD
options.b: A Specialist Advanced exam only, with 2 years of PPD in total
options.c: One Core Practices exam and one further year of study leave
options.d: All eight Specialist Principles exams with no PPD requirement

questions.explanation: To become a Fellow, an Associate passes two Specialist Principles (SP) subjects and one Specialist Advanced (SA) subject, which is the final exam, and completes 3 years of PPD, one more than at Associate level. Option D overstates the SP requirement, B drops the SP exams and gives the Associate PPD total, and C confuses the stages.

questions.topic: History and Professional Structure of Actuarial Science
questions.question: Which of the following IFoA subjects belongs to the Core Practices stage?
questions.explanation: The Core Practices stage consists of CP1 Actuarial Practice, CP2 Modelling Practice and CP3 Communication Practice. CM1 (A) and CB2 (D) are Core Principles subjects taken earlier, and SP2 (C) is a Specialist Principles subject taken on the way to Fellowship.

questions.topic: History and Professional Structure of Actuarial Science
questions.question: Which sequence correctly shows the usual progression of membership grades in an actuarial professional body?
questions.explanation: A person joins as a student while sitting exams, qualifies as an Associate after the earlier stages, and becomes a Fellow, the highest qualified grade, after the final exams and experience. Options A, D and C put the grades in the wrong order.

questions.topic: History and Professional Structure of Actuarial Science
questions.question: Exam FM is one of the preliminary exams recognised by both the SOA and the CAS. What subject does it cover?
questions.explanation: Exam FM (formerly Exam 2) is Financial Mathematics, covering interest, annuities and the time value of money; Exam P is Probability. Options D, B and C are guesses at the letters that do not match the actual exam.

questions.topic: History and Professional Structure of Actuarial Science
questions.question: Which statement best describes a Fellow of the Society of Actuaries (FSA)?

options.a: Has passed only the preliminary probability and financial mathematics exams
options.b: Has registered as a student but has not yet passed any exams
options.c: Has been elected for services to the profession without passing exams
options.d: Has shown knowledge in all major practice areas, with further concentration in one or more of them

questions.explanation: An FSA has demonstrated knowledge across all major practice areas, concentrated further in one or more, and received further education in professionalism. Option A describes an early-stage student, B a new student, and C sounds like honorary membership rather than fellowship.

questions.topic: History and Professional Structure of Actuarial Science
questions.question: Which statement about how actuaries usually qualify is correct?

options.a: They must stop working until every professional exam has been passed
options.b: They qualify by passing one final exam set by the national insurance regulator
options.c: They qualify automatically on completing a first degree in actuarial science
options.d: They pass a series of professional exams, usually while working, so they earn while they learn

questions.explanation: Professional designation comes from passing a series of exams, and most candidates work and study at the same time. A degree (C) may give exemptions but does not qualify anyone by itself, regulators (B) do not set the qualifying exams, and A is the opposite of the usual earn-while-you-learn path.

questions.topic: History and Professional Structure of Actuarial Science
questions.question: A Code of Professional Conduct sets out the responsibilities of actuaries. Which of the following is NOT one of the groups the Code says actuaries have responsibilities to?

options.c: Competing actuarial firms seeking their clients

questions.explanation: The Code identifies responsibilities to the public, to clients and employers, and to the actuarial profession. Options A, B and D are exactly those groups, so the odd one out is competing firms, which the Code does not list.

questions.topic: History and Professional Structure of Actuarial Science
questions.question: In the United States, which body promulgates the Actuarial Standards of Practice (ASOPs) that say what an actuary should consider, document and disclose on an assignment?

options.d: The Institute and Faculty of Actuaries (IFoA)

questions.explanation: The ASB issues the ASOPs used by actuaries working in the United States. The IAA (C) issues model international standards (ISAPs), the CAS (B) is a qualifying body, and the IFoA (D) is a UK body.

questions.topic: History and Professional Structure of Actuarial Science
questions.question: The American Academy of Actuaries was established in 1965. What is the significance of its MAAA designation for actuaries working in the United States?

options.a: It must be held to sign statements of actuarial opinion
options.b: It is the first exam a student must pass to start actuarial training
options.c: It is given only to actuaries who work for the US government
options.d: It replaces the need to hold an SOA or CAS qualification

questions.explanation: MAAA (Member, American Academy of Actuaries) is required before a US actuary can sign statements of actuarial opinion. It is not an exam (B), it does not replace SOA or CAS credentials (D), and it is not limited to government actuaries (C).

questions.topic: History and Professional Structure of Actuarial Science
questions.question: A client in the United States complains that an actuary breached the professional code of conduct. Which body reviews such complaints and can recommend discipline?

options.a: The Actuarial Board for Counseling and Discipline (ABCD)

questions.explanation: The ABCD reviews complaints about possible breaches of the Code, advises actuaries on professional conduct and can recommend discipline. The ASB (D) writes standards rather than hearing complaints, the IAA (C) is an international association of associations, and NAICOM (B) is a Nigerian insurance regulator.

questions.topic: History and Professional Structure of Actuarial Science
questions.question: When actuarial professional bodies were founded in the mid-19th century, what was one of their main purposes besides supporting actuaries?

options.a: Protecting the public by ensuring members' competence and ethical standards
options.b: Setting the premium rates that every insurer had to charge
options.c: Collecting taxes on insurance premiums for the government
options.d: Selling life policies directly to the public

questions.explanation: Professional bodies were created to support actuaries and to protect the public by making sure members are competent and ethical, through exams, codes and standards. Options D and B are insurers' commercial activities, and C is a government function.

questions.topic: History and Professional Structure of Actuarial Science
questions.question: IFoA Specialist Principles subjects reflect the main career areas of actuaries. Which of the following is NOT one of them?
questions.explanation: The Specialist Principles cover Health and Care, Life Insurance, Pensions and Other Benefits, Investment and Finance, Financial Derivatives, General Insurance Reserving, General Insurance Pricing and Enterprise Risk Management. Options B, C and A are on that list, but tax auditing is accounting work, not an actuarial specialism.

questions.topic: History and Professional Structure of Actuarial Science
questions.question: Ngozi works for a consulting firm in Abuja. Her job is to project the salaries and retirement ages of a company's staff and estimate how much must be set aside to pay their future retirement benefits. Which actuarial specialisation is this?
questions.explanation: Projecting members' salaries and retirement benefits and the funding needed for them is pensions work. General insurance pricing (D) sets rates for cover such as motor or fire, financial derivatives (C) values options and similar contracts, and health and care (A) deals with medical and care costs.

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: The international actuarial symbol for the effective rate of interest is ________
questions.explanation: The plain letter i stands for the effective rate of interest per unit time, the actual interest earned on 1 over one period. Option B, i^(m), is the nominal rate convertible m times a year, while C and D are discount rates rather than interest rates.

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: The international actuarial symbol for the nominal rate of interest convertible m times a year is ________
questions.explanation: i^(m) is the nominal rate of interest payable m-thly, meaning interest of i^(m)/m is added every 1/m of a year. Option A (i) is the effective rate, and C and D are the effective and nominal rates of discount.

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: The international actuarial symbol for the effective rate of discount is ________
questions.explanation: d is the effective rate of discount, interest measured against the amount at the end of the period, with d = i/(1 + i). Option D, d^(m), is the nominal rate of discount convertible m times a year, and A and B are interest rates.

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: The international actuarial symbol for the nominal rate of discount convertible m times a year is ________
questions.explanation: d^(m) is the nominal rate of discount payable m-thly, the discount version of i^(m). Option C (d) is the effective annual rate of discount, while A and B are rates of interest.

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: The international actuarial symbol for the present value of a whole life assurance on a life aged x is ________
questions.explanation: A_x is the present value of 1 paid at the end of the year of death of (x), whenever death happens, which is whole life assurance. Option B adds a term n, making it an endowment assurance, and C, with the 1 over the x, is a term assurance that pays only on death within n years.

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: The international actuarial symbol for the present value of an n-year term assurance on a life aged x is ________
questions.explanation: A^1_x:n|, with the 1 over the x, means the benefit is paid only if (x) dies before the n-year term ends, which is term assurance. Option A (A_x) pays on death at any time, and B (A_x:n|) also pays if the life survives to the end of the term, which makes it an endowment.

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: The international actuarial symbol for the present value of an n-year endowment assurance on a life aged x is ________
questions.explanation: A_x:n| pays 1 on death within n years or on survival to the end of the n years, which is an endowment assurance. Option C covers only the death part (term assurance), and A is whole life assurance with no fixed term.

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: The international actuarial symbol for the present value of an n-year temporary life annuity-due on a life aged x (payments at the start of each year while (x) is alive, for at most n years) is ________
questions.explanation: a-double-dot_x:n| is a life annuity: payments of 1 are made at the start of each year while (x) survives, for at most n years, and the two dots show it is paid in advance. Options A, B and C begin with a capital A, which is the symbol for assurances that pay a lump sum on death or maturity rather than a regular income.

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: Use the survival function s(x) = 1 - x/105, 0 <= x <= 105, where s(x) is the probability that a newborn survives to age x. What is the probability that a life aged 0 will survive to age 16?
questions.explanation: The probability of surviving from birth to age 16 is s(16) = 1 - 16/105 = 89/105. Option D (27/105) is the probability of dying between 16 and 43, and C (62/89) is a conditional survival probability for a life already aged 16.

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: Use the survival function s(x) = 1 - x/105, 0 <= x <= 105, where s(x) is the probability that a newborn survives to age x. What is the probability that a life aged 0 will survive to age 43?
questions.explanation: Survival from birth to 43 is s(43) = 1 - 43/105 = 62/105. Option C (62/89) is the probability of reaching 43 given survival to 16, so it uses the wrong starting point, and B (89/105) is survival to age 16 only.

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: Use the survival function s(x) = 1 - x/105, 0 <= x <= 105, where s(x) is the probability that a newborn survives to age x. What is the probability that a life aged 0 will die between ages 16 and 43?
questions.explanation: Dying between 16 and 43 means surviving to 16 but not to 43, so the probability is s(16) - s(43) = 89/105 - 62/105 = 27/105. Options A and B are the probabilities of surviving to 43 and to 16, not of dying in between.

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: Use the survival function s(x) = 1 - x/105, 0 <= x <= 105, where s(x) is the probability that a newborn survives to age x. What is the probability that a life aged 16 will survive to age 43?
questions.explanation: Since the life has already reached 16, divide: s(43)/s(16) = (62/105)/(89/105) = 62/89. Option A (62/105) is the probability measured from birth and ignores the fact that the life has already survived to 16.

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: Use the survival function s(x) = sqrt(100 - x)/10, 0 <= x <= 100, where s(x) is the probability that a newborn survives to age x. What is the probability of surviving from birth to age 64?
questions.explanation: s(64) = sqrt(100 - 64)/10 = sqrt(36)/10 = 6/10 = 3/5. Option B (4/5) is s(36), survival to age 36, so it uses the wrong age.

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: Use the survival function s(x) = sqrt(100 - x)/10, 0 <= x <= 100, where s(x) is the probability that a newborn survives to age x. What is the probability of surviving from birth to age 36?
questions.explanation: s(36) = sqrt(100 - 36)/10 = sqrt(64)/10 = 8/10 = 4/5. Option A (3/5) is s(64), survival to the older age of 64.

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: Use the survival function s(x) = sqrt(100 - x)/10, 0 <= x <= 100, where s(x) is the probability that a newborn survives to age x. What is the probability that a life aged 36 will survive to age 64?
questions.explanation: For a life already aged 36, the probability is s(64)/s(36) = (6/10)/(8/10) = 3/4. Option A (2/10) is the difference s(36) - s(64), which is the chance that a newborn dies between 36 and 64, not a conditional survival probability.

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: Use the survival function s(x) = sqrt(100 - x)/10, 0 <= x <= 100, where s(x) is the probability that a newborn survives to age x. What is the probability that a life aged 0 will die between ages 36 and 64?
questions.explanation: A newborn dies between 36 and 64 if it reaches 36 but not 64, so the probability is s(36) - s(64) = 4/5 - 3/5 = 1/5. Options A and B are the probabilities of surviving to 64 and to 36, not of dying between them.

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: Use this extract from a hypothetical life table: age x = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 with l_x = 100,000; 99,499; 98,995; 98,489; 97,980; 97,468; 96,954 and d_x = 501; 504; 506; 509; 512; 514; 517. What is the value of p_4, the probability that a life aged 4 survives one year? (4 decimal places.)
questions.explanation: p_4 = l_5/l_4 = 97,468/97,980 = 0.99477, which rounds to 0.9948. Option C (0.9984) and D (0.9985) swap or misplace digits, and B (0.9848) would imply far more deaths than the 512 shown in the table.

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: Use this extract from a hypothetical life table: age x = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 with l_x = 100,000; 99,499; 98,995; 98,489; 97,980; 97,468; 96,954 and d_x = 501; 504; 506; 509; 512; 514; 517. What is the value of q_4, the probability that a life aged 4 dies within one year? (5 decimal places.)
questions.explanation: q_4 = d_4/l_4 = 512/97,980 = 0.005226, which rounds to 0.00523. Option A (0.00525) wrongly divides by l_5 instead of l_4, option B (0.00517) uses the age-3 figures, and option D is p_4, the probability of surviving rather than dying.

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: Use this extract from a hypothetical life table: age x = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 with l_x = 100,000; 99,499; 98,995; 98,489; 97,980; 97,468; 96,954 and d_x = 501; 504; 506; 509; 512; 514; 517. What is the value of _2p_3, the probability that a life aged 3 survives 2 years to age 5? (4 decimal places.)
questions.explanation: _2p_3 = l_5/l_3 = 97,468/98,489 = 0.98963, which rounds to 0.9896. Options A (0.9986) and C (0.9996) are too close to 1 for two years of survival given more than 1,000 deaths, and D (0.8996) is far too low.

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: Use this extract from a hypothetical life table: age x = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 with l_x = 100,000; 99,499; 98,995; 98,489; 97,980; 97,468; 96,954 and d_x = 501; 504; 506; 509; 512; 514; 517. What is the value of _2q_2, the probability that a life aged 2 dies within 2 years? (5 decimal places.)
questions.explanation: _2q_2 = (l_2 - l_4)/l_2 = (98,995 - 97,980)/98,995 = 1,015/98,995 = 0.01025. Option A (0.10250) and B (0.00125) misplace the decimal point, and D (0.11025) is far too large for a two-year death probability when only about 1,000 of nearly 99,000 lives die.

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: What is the life table used for?

options.c: Predicting the future value of an investment

questions.explanation: A life table shows how a group of lives shrinks with age, so it is used to analyse mortality and survival patterns, such as the chance of living from one age to the next. Option B is a general description of multi-state models, and option A is done with interest rates and discount factors, not the life table alone.

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: In a life table, what does the l_x column represent?

options.a: Number of individuals alive at exact age x
options.b: Probability of surviving to age x
options.c: Number of individuals who died at age x
options.d: Cumulative survival probability up to age x

questions.explanation: l_x is the number of lives still alive at exact age x out of the starting group. Option B is l_x divided by l_0, a probability rather than a count, and option C is d_x, the number dying between ages x and x+1.

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: In a life table, l_0 = 1,000 and l_1 = 900. What is the probability of surviving from age 0 to age 1, p_0?
questions.explanation: The survival probability is p_0 = l_1/l_0 = 900/1000 = 0.9. Option A is q_0, the probability of dying in the first year, and option D wrongly treats 0.9 as a percentage, which would be 100 times too small.

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: In a life table, l_0 = 1,000 and l_1 = 900. What is the probability that a life aged 0 dies before reaching age 1, q_0?
questions.explanation: First find d_0 = l_0 - l_1 = 1000 - 900 = 100 deaths, then q_0 = d_0/l_0 = 100/1000 = 0.1. Option B is p_0, the survival probability, and option D is d_0, the number of deaths rather than a probability.

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: In the international actuarial notation, the lower space to the RIGHT of a principal symbol (as in q_x) is reserved for signs indicating which of the following?

options.a: The ages of the lives and the order of succession of events
options.b: Any other notion the user wishes to add
options.d: The duration of the operation and its position in time

questions.explanation: The lower right space carries the age conditions, which is why the age x sits there in l_x, q_x and A_x, and it also shows the order in which lives fail. Option D describes the lower left space, Option C the upper right space and Option B the upper left space.

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: Under the general principles of the international actuarial notation, which position around a principal symbol is reserved for signs showing the duration of the operation and its position with regard to time?

options.a: The upper space to the right
options.b: The lower space to the left
options.c: The lower space to the right
options.d: The upper space to the left

questions.explanation: Duration and timing conditions go in the lower left, which is why the n in a term such as 5p_x or the deferment m in m|q_x is written before the main letter. Option C is for ages, Option A is for periodicity and Option D is left free for other notions.

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: In the symbol i^(m), the m is written in the upper space to the right of i. In the international actuarial notation this position indicates which of the following?

options.a: The length of the term-certain in years
options.b: The age of the life involved
options.c: The order in which the lives are to fail
options.d: The periodicity of the events, for example how often interest is convertible

questions.explanation: The upper right space is reserved for periodicity, so i^(m) means a nominal rate convertible m times a year. Option B belongs in the lower right space, Option A is shown by the angle n| and Option C is shown by numerals over or under the suffix.

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: Which of the following statements about the upper space to the LEFT of a principal symbol in the international actuarial notation is correct?

options.a: It is reserved for the duration of the operation
options.b: It is reserved for the frequency of payment
options.c: It is free, and signs for other notions can be placed in it
options.d: It is reserved for the ages of the lives involved

questions.explanation: The upper left space is the one position the system leaves free, so other notions can be placed there when needed. Option D is the lower right space, Option B is the upper right space and Option A is the lower left space.

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: In actuarial notation, what does the symbol (x), a letter enclosed in brackets, denote?

options.a: The probability of dying at age x
options.c: The number of persons living at age x

questions.explanation: A letter in round brackets, such as (x) or (40), stands for a life of that age, so (x) is read as 'a person aged x'. Option C is l_x, Option A is q_x, and Option B would be shown by an angle, as in n|.

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: In the symbols a_n| and s_n|, the n written inside a right-angle mark (n|) indicates which of the following?

options.a: A deferment of n years after death
options.b: Payments made n times a year

questions.explanation: The right-angle mark around n shows a fixed term of n years that does not depend on anyone being alive, so a_n| is an annuity-certain for n years. Option C would be written (n), and Option B is a periodicity sign that goes in the upper right space.

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: Which actuarial symbol denotes the total interest earned on 1 in a year, assuming any interest received more often than yearly is reinvested immediately on the same terms as the original principal?
questions.explanation: This is the definition of i, the effective rate of interest per year. Option A, d, is the discount on 1 due a year hence, Option D, v, is the present value of 1 due a year hence, and Option B, delta, is the force of interest.

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: In actuarial notation, what does the symbol v represent?

options.a: The present value of 1 due a year hence
options.b: The accumulated value of 1 after one year
options.c: The nominal rate of interest convertible m times a year
options.d: The discount on 1 due a year hence

questions.explanation: v is the discount factor, v = 1/(1+i): the amount needed now to have 1 in one year's time. Option D is d = 1 - v, Option B is 1 + i, and Option C is i^(m).

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: In actuarial notation, the symbol d (when used with interest) stands for which of the following?

options.a: The discount on 1 due a year hence
options.b: The present value of 1 due a year hence
options.c: The number of persons dying at age x

questions.explanation: In interest theory, d is the effective rate of discount: the discount allowed when 1 due in a year is paid now, so d = 1 - v. Option B is v. Option C is also written with the letter d, but in the mortality table it carries an age suffix, as in d_x.

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: Which symbol is used in actuarial notation for the force of interest, the instantaneous rate of growth that acts like a nominal rate compounded continuously?
questions.explanation: The force of interest is written delta, and it satisfies 1 + i = e^delta. Option C, mu, is the force of mortality, Option D is a nominal rate convertible m times a year, and Option A, m, is the central death rate.

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: A Lagos bank quotes a savings product at '12% per annum convertible monthly'. Written in standard actuarial notation, this quoted rate is
questions.explanation: A rate convertible m times a year is a nominal rate, written i^(m), so monthly conversion gives i^(12) = 0.12. Option C would mean 12% effective a year, which is lower than the true effective rate here, and Option A would mean continuous compounding.

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: In a mortality table, which symbol gives the number of persons who attain exact age x?
questions.explanation: l_x (l for 'living') is the number of the original group who survive to exact age x. Option A counts those who die between ages x and x+1, Option B is a probability rather than a number, and Option D is the expectation of life.

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: In a mortality table, d_x = l_x - l_(x+1). What does d_x measure?

options.a: The number of persons who die between ages x and x+1
options.b: The present value of an assurance on a life aged x
options.c: The number of persons alive at age x+1
options.d: The probability that a person aged x dies within one year

questions.explanation: d_x is a count: the people alive at age x minus those still alive at x+1, which gives the number who die during that year of age. Option D is q_x = d_x / l_x, a probability rather than a count, and Option C is l_(x+1).

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: Which symbol denotes the probability that a person aged x will die within one year?
questions.explanation: q_x is the one-year probability of dying for (x), and it equals d_x / l_x. Option C is the probability of surviving the year, Option B is the number who die, not a probability, and Option A is the force of mortality.

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: For a life aged x, which relationship between p_x and q_x always holds?
questions.explanation: Within one year a life aged x either survives (probability p_x) or dies (probability q_x), so the two probabilities add up to 1. Option D would force p_x to be greater than 1, which is impossible for a probability, and Options C and B do not describe how survival and death share the year.

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: Among the fundamental symbolic letters for mortality tables, which letter stands for the force of mortality?
questions.explanation: The Greek letter mu (written mu_x at age x) is the force of mortality, the instantaneous rate of dying. Option B, m, is the central death rate, Option C, q, is the probability of dying, and Option A, delta, is the force of interest.

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: Which of the following pairs of fundamental actuarial letters and meanings is NOT correctly matched?

options.a: A = present value of an assurance
options.d: s = present value of an annuity

questions.explanation: In the notation, s is the amount (accumulated value) of an annuity, and a is the present value of an annuity, so the pairing in this option is wrong. Options A, B and C are all correct pairings from the list of fundamental symbols.

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: Which fundamental actuarial letter denotes the present value of an endowment, that is, a sum paid only if the life survives to the end of a stated period?
questions.explanation: E stands for the present value of a pure endowment. Option D, A, is the present value of an assurance (paid on death), Option A, small e, is the expectation of life, and Option C, P, is a premium.

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: In the international actuarial notation, the symbol e_x (with no mark above the e) denotes which of the following?

options.a: The curtate expectation of life (average after-lifetime) of (x)
options.b: The number of persons who die at age x
options.c: The complete expectation of life of (x)
options.d: The present value of an endowment on (x)

questions.explanation: e_x without a mark is the curtate expectation of life, which counts only complete future years lived by (x). Option C is shown by a small circle over the e, Option D is capital E, and Option B is d_x.

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: When a small circle is placed over the letter e in the expectation-of-life symbol, what does the circle indicate?

options.a: That the life is a select life
options.b: That payments are made at the beginning of each year
options.c: That the expectation is complete rather than curtate

questions.explanation: A small circle over a principal symbol means the benefit is complete, so e with a circle is the complete expectation of life. Option D is shown by a bar over the symbol, Option A by square brackets around the age, and Option B by the trema (two dots).

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: A horizontal bar placed over a principal symbol, as in A-bar_x, indicates which of the following?

options.a: The benefit is complete rather than curtate
options.b: The benefit is payable at the beginning of each year
options.c: The benefit is continuous or payable at the moment of death
options.d: The benefit is on the last survivor of several lives

questions.explanation: A bar over the main letter means the payments are continuous (momently), so A-bar_x is an assurance payable at the moment of death. Option A is shown by a small circle, Option B by the trema (two dots), and Option D by a bar over the suffix, not over the main letter.

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: The diaeresis or trema (two dots) placed above a or s, as in a-double-dot_n| (the annuity-due), is a symbol of
questions.explanation: The two dots show that each payment is brought forward by one period, so an annuity-due pays at the start of each year instead of the end. Option A is shown by a bar, Option B by a small circle and Option C by square brackets around the age.

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: Which symbol denotes the amount (accumulated value at the end of the term) of an annuity-certain of 1 per annum for n years, payments made at the END of each year?
questions.explanation: s_n| is the accumulated value at time n of payments of 1 made at the end of each year for n years. Option C, a_n|, is the present value of the same annuity, and Options A and D are for annuities-due, which pay at the beginning of each year.

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: The 1949 revision of the international actuarial notation introduced the symbol s-double-dot_n|. What does it represent?

options.a: The present value of a continuous annuity
options.b: The present value of an annuity-due
options.c: The accumulated amount of an annuity paid at the end of each year
options.d: The accumulated amount at the end of the term of an annuity-due

questions.explanation: Adopting the trema for annuities-due made room for s-double-dot_n|, the accumulated amount of an annuity-due at the end of the term, which previously had no symbol. Option B is a-double-dot_n|, Option C is s_n| and Option A is a-bar_n|.

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: In actuarial notation, two or more letters written in a suffix without any distinguishing mark, as in a_xyz, indicate which of the following?

options.a: The last survivor of the lives
options.b: Joint lives, so the status lasts while all the lives survive
options.c: The order in which the lives must die
options.d: A reversionary benefit after the first death

questions.explanation: Letters placed side by side in the suffix mean joint lives, so a_xyz is paid at the end of each year while (x), (y) and (z) are all alive. Option A needs a horizontal bar over the suffix, Option D uses a perpendicular bar, and Option C uses numerals over or under the suffix.

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: Why is a colon, rather than a point or a comma, used to separate items in a suffix such as a_(x:n|)?

options.a: To show that the benefit is deferred
options.b: To show that the lives are last survivors
options.c: To show that the life was select at entry
options.d: To avoid confusion with decimals when numbers are involved

questions.explanation: The colon only separates the items in the suffix. A point or comma could be misread as a decimal point when the ages are numbers, as in a_(40:10|). The other options describe marks with other jobs: a horizontal bar for survivors, a vertical bar or left subscript for deferment, and square brackets for selection.

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: What does the symbol a_(x:n|) represent?

options.b: A whole-life annuity on (x) deferred n years
options.c: A temporary life annuity on (x) for n years
options.d: An endowment assurance on (x) for n years

questions.explanation: The status x:n| lasts for the joint duration of the life of (x) and a term of n years, so the annuity stops at death or after n years, whichever comes first. This is a temporary annuity. Option A ignores the life, Option B would need a deferment sign on the left, and Option D is A_(x:n|).

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: A Nigerian life office sells a 15-year policy to a 35-year-old: N2,000,000 is paid at the end of the year of death if death occurs within 15 years, or at the end of 15 years if the policyholder is then alive. Ignoring the sum assured, the actuarial symbol for this benefit is
questions.explanation: The policy pays on death within the term OR on survival to the end of it, which is an endowment assurance, A_(x:n|), here with x = 35 and n = 15. Option C is a whole-life assurance with no term, Option D is a temporary annuity, and Option B has no term shown and covers survival only.

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: In actuarial notation a perpendicular (vertical) bar separating the lives in a suffix, as in a_(y|x), means that the status after the bar follows the status before it. a_(y|x) is therefore

options.a: an annuity to (y) payable after the death of (x)
options.b: an annuity payable while at least one of (x) and (y) is alive
options.c: a reversionary annuity to (x) payable after the death of (y)

questions.explanation: With a vertical bar, the status after the bar (x) takes over when the status before it (y) fails, so payments to (x) begin after (y) dies. Option D would be written a_xy, Option B needs a horizontal bar over xy, and Option A reverses the order.

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: A horizontal bar over the suffix with a number above it shows how many survivors are needed. What is the difference between writing 2 and writing [2] above the bar for three lives (x), (y) and (z)?

options.a: 2 means exactly two survivors; [2] means at least two survivors
options.b: There is no difference; the brackets are optional
options.c: 2 means at least two survivors; [2] means exactly two survivors
options.d: 2 means two joint lives; [2] means two reversionary lives

questions.explanation: A plain number r over the bar means at least r survivors, while the same number in square brackets means exactly r survivors. If no number is shown, at least one survivor is meant. Option A swaps the two meanings, and Option B is wrong because the brackets change the meaning.

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: In the symbol A^1_(xy), with the numeral 1 placed over the x, what does the numeral show?

options.a: The assurance is paid on the first death of either life
options.b: The assurance is paid at the end of the year of death of (x) only if (x) dies first of the two lives
options.c: The assurance is paid if exactly one life survives
options.d: The assurance covers one year only

questions.explanation: Numerals over or under the suffix give the order in which the lives must fail, so 1 over x means the benefit is paid on (x)'s death only if (x) dies before (y). Option A would be a joint-life assurance A_xy, Option D confuses the numeral with a term, and Option C is a survivorship symbol with [1] over a bar.

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: If the age suffix of an actuarial symbol is enclosed in square brackets, as in l_[x]+t, what does this indicate?

options.b: The life is one of several joint lives
options.c: The age has been rounded to the nearest birthday
options.d: Selection: the life was selected at age x and t years have passed since selection

questions.explanation: Square brackets around the age mark the age at selection, and the number outside the brackets is the time since selection. So l_[x]+t is the number in the select table, selected at age x, who have reached age x + t. Option B uses plain letters in the suffix and Option A uses a bar over the main letter.

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: In select-table notation, a_[x-n]+n denotes the value of an annuity on a life

options.a: now aged x who is select today
options.b: now aged x who was selected n years ago at age x - n
options.c: now aged x - n who will be selected in n years
options.d: aged x + n who was selected at age x

questions.explanation: The age inside the brackets is the age at selection (x - n), and adding n gives the present age x. Option A describes a_[x], a life aged x who is select now, and Option C turns the time order around.

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: In the international actuarial notation, a single accent and a double accent on the premium symbol (P' and P'') are used to denote, respectively,

options.a: a premium paid monthly, and a premium paid quarterly
options.b: the office premium, and the net premium
options.c: a valuation premium other than the net premium, and the office (commercial) premium
options.d: a single premium, and an annual premium

questions.explanation: Accents mark modified premiums: P' is a premium other than the net premium used in a valuation, and P'' is the office (commercial) premium. Option B gets the pairs wrong, and Option A confuses accents with periodicity, which is written in the upper right space.

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: In compound actuarial symbols, (Ia) denotes

options.a: an annuity whose payments vary irregularly
options.b: an annuity starting at 1 and increasing by 1 per annum
options.c: an annuity paid at the beginning of each year
options.d: an annuity starting at n and decreasing by 1 per annum

questions.explanation: The letter I in front of a symbol means an increasing benefit, so (Ia) pays 1, 2, 3 and so on. Option D uses D for decreasing, Option A uses the varying symbol, and Option C is shown by the trema, not by I.

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: The 1949 revision of the international actuarial notation brought in several changes. Which of the following was NOT one of them?

options.a: Adopting a-double-dot for an annuity-due (first payment made at once)
options.b: Replacing j(m) with i^(m) for the nominal rate of interest
options.c: Adopting U as the official international symbol for a surrender value
options.d: Introducing D in compound symbols for decreasing benefits

questions.explanation: A proposal to make U the official symbol for the surrender value was not adopted. It was only agreed that U should be chosen if a symbol were ever needed. Options B, A and D were all listed among the changes introduced.

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: The existing international actuarial notation was set out in an explanatory statement that was unanimously adopted at which gathering?

options.b: The Second International Actuarial Congress, London, 1898
options.c: The Eleventh International Actuarial Congress, Paris, 1937
options.d: The Third International Actuarial Congress, Paris, 1900

questions.explanation: The notation, based on George King's 'Key to the Notation', was adopted unanimously at the Second International Actuarial Congress in London in May 1898. Option D was where Dr Sprague's rearranged statement was submitted, Option C only appointed a committee on notation, and Option A never took place because of the war.

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: In the context of life tables, mortality is best described as

options.a: the process of deciding whether to accept a risk for insurance
options.b: the number of persons alive at each exact age
options.c: the average number of years a newborn is expected to live
options.d: the incidence of death in a population, often measured by the probability that an individual dies within a period

questions.explanation: Mortality is the incidence of death in a population. It is usually measured by probabilities of dying such as q_x, which is exactly what a mortality (life) table gives. Option C is the expectation of life, Option B is the l_x column, and Option A is selection.

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: An actuary at a Lagos life insurer is pricing a new term assurance and needs the probability that a 45-year-old policyholder dies within the next year. Which column of a life table gives this directly?
questions.explanation: The q_x column gives the one-year probability of death for a life aged x, which is the key mortality input for pricing term cover. Option D gives numbers alive and Option C gives numbers dying, which must be divided by l_x to get a probability. Option B gives the average future lifetime.

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a characteristic of a standard life (mortality) table built from a radix l_0?

options.b: d_x = l_x - l_(x+1) for each age
options.c: The l_x column increases as age increases
options.d: The sum of d_x from age x to the end of the table equals l_x

questions.explanation: Nobody joins the group after birth and people leave it only by dying, so l_x can only stay the same or fall as x rises. Options B and A are basic relations of the table, and Option D holds because everyone alive at age x must die at some later age.

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: In a life table, the starting number l_0, chosen as a convenient round figure such as 100,000, is called the
questions.explanation: The radix is the arbitrary starting size of the group at age 0, from which every later l_x is worked out. Option A, m_x, and Option B, mu_x, are measures of mortality, and Option C is the age by which nobody is left (l_x = 0).

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: The curtate expectation of life e_x can be described as the value of a life annuity a_x (payments of 1 at the end of each year while (x) is alive) when it is valued at which rate of interest?
questions.explanation: If i = 0, every payment of 1 is worth exactly 1 today, so a_x just counts the expected number of future anniversaries survived, which is e_x. The other options do not reduce a_x to a simple count of years survived.

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: A 2022 review of the Nigerian actuarial market noted that there were 'no local actuarial tables'. What is the main practical consequence for Nigerian life insurers?

options.a: Their q_x and l_x values must be based on mortality tables built from other populations
options.b: Their annuities must all be annuities-due
options.c: They must price all life policies without interest
options.d: They cannot use the symbol l_x in their calculations

questions.explanation: Without a local life table, insurers have to use or adapt foreign mortality tables, which may not reflect Nigerian mortality, for their survival and death probabilities. The other options do not follow, because notation, interest and payment timing do not depend on whether a local table exists.

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: An extract from a life table gives: l_50 = 10,000; l_51 = 9,850; l_52 = 9,682; l_53 = 9,494; l_54 = 9,283; l_55 = 9,046. Calculate d_52, the number of persons dying between exact ages 52 and 53.
questions.explanation: d_52 = l_52 - l_53 = 9,682 - 9,494 = 188. Option A is d_51 (the wrong year), Option B is d_53, and Option D counts all the deaths from age 50 to 53.

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: An extract from a life table gives: l_50 = 10,000; l_51 = 9,850; l_52 = 9,682; l_53 = 9,494; l_54 = 9,283; l_55 = 9,046. Calculate q_51, correct to 5 decimal places.
questions.explanation: q_51 = d_51 / l_51 = (9,850 - 9,682)/9,850 = 168/9,850 = 0.01706. Option A divides by l_52 instead of l_51, Option D is p_51, and Option B uses the deaths at age 50.

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: An extract from a life table gives: l_50 = 10,000; l_51 = 9,850; l_52 = 9,682; l_53 = 9,494; l_54 = 9,283; l_55 = 9,046. Calculate p_53, the probability that a life aged 53 survives one year, correct to 5 decimal places.
questions.explanation: p_53 = l_54 / l_53 = 9,283/9,494 = 0.97778. Option A is q_53 = 1 - p_53, Option C is p_52 (one year too early), and Option D wrongly divides by the radix of this extract, l_50.

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: An extract from a life table gives: l_50 = 10,000; l_51 = 9,850; l_52 = 9,682; l_53 = 9,494; l_54 = 9,283; l_55 = 9,046. Calculate 3p50, the probability that a life aged 50 survives to age 53, correct to 4 decimal places.
questions.explanation: 3p50 = l_53 / l_50 = 9,494/10,000 = 0.9494. Option D uses l_52 (only 2 years), Option C uses l_54 (4 years), and Option A is 3q50, the probability of dying instead.

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: An extract from a life table gives: l_50 = 10,000; l_51 = 9,850; l_52 = 9,682; l_53 = 9,494; l_54 = 9,283; l_55 = 9,046. Calculate 2q51, the probability that a life aged 51 dies before age 53, correct to 4 decimal places.
questions.explanation: 2q51 = (l_51 - l_53)/l_51 = (9,850 - 9,494)/9,850 = 356/9,850 = 0.0361. Option D counts only one year of deaths (q_51), Option C divides by l_50 instead of l_51, and Option B is 2p51.

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: An extract from a life table gives: l_50 = 10,000; l_51 = 9,850; l_52 = 9,682; l_53 = 9,494; l_54 = 9,283; l_55 = 9,046. Calculate 2|q50, the probability that a life aged 50 survives 2 years and then dies in the following year (between ages 52 and 53), correct to 5 decimal places.
questions.explanation: 2|q50 = d_52 / l_50 = (9,682 - 9,494)/10,000 = 188/10,000 = 0.01880. Option C is q_52, which divides by l_52 and so ignores the need to survive from 50 to 52. Option D is 3q50 (death at any time in 3 years), and Option A uses the deaths in the wrong year.

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: An extract from a life table gives: l_50 = 10,000; l_51 = 9,850; l_52 = 9,682; l_53 = 9,494; l_54 = 9,283; l_55 = 9,046. Calculate 1|3q50, the probability that a life aged 50 survives to age 51 and then dies before age 54, correct to 4 decimal places.
questions.explanation: 1|3q50 = (l_51 - l_54)/l_50 = (9,850 - 9,283)/10,000 = 0.0567. Option C divides by l_51 and so ignores surviving the first year, Option A counts deaths from age 50, and Option B runs the 3-year death window one year too long.

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: A life table gives: l_20 = 100,000; l_21 = 99,820; l_22 = 99,630; l_23 = 99,428; l_24 = 99,213; l_25 = 98,985. A Lagos firm employs 2,500 people, all aged exactly 20. Using the table, how many of them are expected to be alive at age 24 (to the nearest whole number)?
questions.explanation: Expected survivors = 2,500 x 4p20 = 2,500 x 99,213/100,000 = 2480.32, about 2,480. Option A uses l_23 (3 years), Option B uses l_25 (5 years), and Option C is the expected number of deaths.

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: A life table gives: l_20 = 100,000; l_21 = 99,820; l_22 = 99,630; l_23 = 99,428; l_24 = 99,213; l_25 = 98,985. A group of 4,000 lives are all aged exactly 22. Calculate the expected number of deaths among them before age 23, correct to 2 decimal places.
questions.explanation: Expected deaths = 4,000 x q_22 = 4,000 x (99,630 - 99,428)/99,630 = 4,000 x 202/99,630 = 8.11. Option A uses q_21, Option B divides by l_20 instead of l_22, and Option C uses q_23.

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: A life table gives: l_20 = 100,000; l_21 = 99,820; l_22 = 99,630; l_23 = 99,428; l_24 = 99,213; l_25 = 98,985. Calculate 4p21, correct to 5 decimal places.
questions.explanation: 4p21 = l_25 / l_21 = 98,985/99,820 = 0.99163. Option B uses l_24 (3 years only), Option C starts from the wrong age (l_20), and Option A is 4q21.

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: A life table gives: l_20 = 100,000; l_21 = 99,820; l_22 = 99,630; l_23 = 99,428; l_24 = 99,213; l_25 = 98,985. Calculate 1|2q20, the probability that a life aged 20 survives one year and then dies within the next 2 years, correct to 5 decimal places.
questions.explanation: 1|2q20 = (l_21 - l_23)/l_20 = (99,820 - 99,428)/100,000 = 392/100,000 = 0.00392. Option B counts only one year of deaths (1|q20), Option D is 2q20 with no deferment, and Option A is 3q20.

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: A life table gives: l_20 = 100,000; l_21 = 99,820; l_22 = 99,630; l_23 = 99,428; l_24 = 99,213; l_25 = 98,985. How many of the lives alive at age 20 in this table die between exact ages 20 and 23?
questions.explanation: Deaths between 20 and 23 = d_20 + d_21 + d_22 = l_20 - l_23 = 100,000 - 99,428 = 572. Option C stops at age 22, Option B runs to age 24, and Option A starts counting from age 21.

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: A life table gives: l_60 = 80,000; l_61 = 78,400; l_62 = 76,560; l_63 = 74,480; l_64 = 72,100; l_65 = 69,450. Calculate q_62, correct to 4 decimal places.
questions.explanation: q_62 = d_62 / l_62 = (76,560 - 74,480)/76,560 = 2,080/76,560 = 0.0272. Option C divides by l_63, Option A is q_61, and Option D divides by l_60, which gives 2|q60 instead.

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: A life table gives: l_60 = 80,000; l_61 = 78,400; l_62 = 76,560; l_63 = 74,480; l_64 = 72,100; l_65 = 69,450. Calculate 5p60, correct to 4 decimal places.
questions.explanation: 5p60 = l_65 / l_60 = 69,450/80,000 = 0.8681. Option D uses l_64 (4 years), Option B is 5q60, and Option A starts at age 61.

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: A life table gives: l_60 = 80,000; l_61 = 78,400; l_62 = 76,560; l_63 = 74,480; l_64 = 72,100; l_65 = 69,450. Calculate 2|q61, the probability that a life aged 61 dies between exact ages 63 and 64, correct to 5 decimal places.
questions.explanation: 2|q61 = d_63 / l_61 = (74,480 - 72,100)/78,400 = 2,380/78,400 = 0.03036. Option B is q_63 (it ignores the 2-year deferment), Option D uses d_62, and Option C is 3q61 (death at any time before 64).

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: A life table gives: l_60 = 80,000; l_61 = 78,400; l_62 = 76,560; l_63 = 74,480; l_64 = 72,100; l_65 = 69,450. Calculate the probability that a life now aged 60 dies between exact ages 63 and 65 (that is, 3|2q60), correct to 4 decimal places.
questions.explanation: 3|2q60 = (l_63 - l_65)/l_60 = (74,480 - 69,450)/80,000 = 5,030/80,000 = 0.0629. Option C divides by l_63, Option A is 5q60, and Option D counts only one year of deaths.

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: A life table gives: l_60 = 80,000; l_61 = 78,400; l_62 = 76,560; l_63 = 74,480; l_64 = 72,100; l_65 = 69,450. A Nigerian pension scheme has 1,200 pensioners, all aged exactly 61. How many deaths are expected among them before age 62 (to the nearest whole number)?
questions.explanation: Expected deaths = 1,200 x q_61 = 1,200 x (78,400 - 76,560)/78,400 = 1,200 x 1,840/78,400 = 28.16, about 28. Option C uses q_60, Option D is the expected number of survivors, and Option A uses 2q61.

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: The last rows of a life table are: l_95 = 1,000; l_96 = 620; l_97 = 340; l_98 = 150; l_99 = 45; l_100 = 0 (no one survives beyond age 100). The curtate expectation of life is e_x = (l_(x+1) + l_(x+2) + ...)/l_x. Calculate e_95, correct to 2 decimal places.
questions.explanation: e_95 = (620 + 340 + 150 + 45 + 0)/1,000 = 1,155/1,000 = 1.16. Option D wrongly includes l_95 in the sum, Option C adds half a year, which gives the approximate complete expectation, and Option A divides by l_96 instead of l_95.

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: The last rows of a life table are: l_95 = 1,000; l_96 = 620; l_97 = 340; l_98 = 150; l_99 = 45; l_100 = 0 (no one survives beyond age 100). Using e_x = (l_(x+1) + l_(x+2) + ...)/l_x, calculate the curtate expectation of life e_97, correct to 2 decimal places.
questions.explanation: e_97 = (150 + 45 + 0)/340 = 195/340 = 0.57. Option B wrongly includes l_97 in the numerator, Option A counts only the first future year (p_97), and Option D divides by l_95 instead of l_97.

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: The last rows of a life table are: l_95 = 1,000; l_96 = 620; l_97 = 340; l_98 = 150; l_99 = 45; l_100 = 0 (no one survives beyond age 100). Calculate the probability that a life now aged 95 dies between exact ages 97 and 98, correct to 2 decimal places.
questions.explanation: 2|q95 = d_97 / l_95 = (340 - 150)/1,000 = 0.19. Option C is q_97 (it ignores surviving from 95 to 97), Option B is 3q95, and Option D uses d_96.

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: In a life table, l_70 = 5,000, d_70 = 150, d_71 = 170, d_72 = 195 and d_73 = 220. Find l_73.
questions.explanation: Since l_(x+1) = l_x - d_x, l_73 = 5,000 - 150 - 170 - 195 = 4,485. Option A is l_72 (one subtraction short), Option B is l_74 (it also subtracts d_73), and Option D adds the deaths instead of subtracting them.

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: In a life table, l_70 = 5,000, d_70 = 150, d_71 = 170, d_72 = 195 and d_73 = 220. Calculate q_71, correct to 5 decimal places.
questions.explanation: First l_71 = 5,000 - 150 = 4,850, so q_71 = d_71 / l_71 = 170/4,850 = 0.03505. Option C divides by l_70 (the step of finding l_71 is missed), Option D divides by l_72, and Option A is p_71.

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: In a life table, l_70 = 5,000, d_70 = 150, d_71 = 170, d_72 = 195 and d_73 = 220. Calculate 3p70, correct to 4 decimal places.
questions.explanation: 3p70 = l_73 / l_70 = (5,000 - 150 - 170 - 195)/5,000 = 4,485/5,000 = 0.8970. Option D covers only 2 years, Option C covers 4 years, and Option B is 3q70.

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: In a life table, l_70 = 5,000, d_70 = 150, d_71 = 170, d_72 = 195 and d_73 = 220. Calculate 3|q70, the probability that a life aged 70 dies between exact ages 73 and 74, correct to 4 decimal places.
questions.explanation: 3|q70 = d_73 / l_70 = 220/5,000 = 0.0440. Option B is q_73 = 220/4,485, which ignores surviving from 70 to 73, Option C is 4q70, and Option D uses d_72.

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: A mortality table gives l_40 = 50,000, q_40 = 0.002, q_41 = 0.0025 and q_42 = 0.003. Calculate d_40, the expected number dying between ages 40 and 41.
questions.explanation: d_40 = l_40 x q_40 = 50,000 x 0.002 = 100. Option D uses q_41, Option B is l_41 (the survivors), and Option A misreads 0.002 as 2%.

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: A mortality table gives l_40 = 50,000, q_40 = 0.002, q_41 = 0.0025 and q_42 = 0.003. Calculate l_43, correct to 2 decimal places.
questions.explanation: l_43 = l_40 x p_40 x p_41 x p_42 = 50,000 x 0.998 x 0.9975 x 0.997 = 49,625.92. Option D is l_42 (one year short), Option B subtracts the three q's from 1 instead of multiplying the p's, and Option C applies one extra year of mortality.

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: For a life aged 40, q_40 = 0.002, q_41 = 0.0025 and q_42 = 0.003. Calculate 3p40, correct to 5 decimal places.
questions.explanation: 3p40 = p_40 x p_41 x p_42 = 0.998 x 0.9975 x 0.997 = 0.99252. Option B subtracts the q's from 1 (a close but wrong shortcut), Option C covers only 2 years, and Option A is 3q40.

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: For a life aged 30, q_30 = 0.004 and q_31 = 0.0045. Calculate 2q30, the probability of dying within 2 years, correct to 6 decimal places.
questions.explanation: 2q30 = 1 - p_30 x p_31 = 1 - 0.996 x 0.9955 = 0.008482. Option B just adds the q's, which counts some lives twice, Option A multiplies the q's (that would be dying in both years, which is impossible), and Option C is 2p30.

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: A life table has radix l_0 = 1,000, with q_0 = 0.05, q_1 = 0.02 and q_2 = 0.01. Calculate l_3, correct to 2 decimal places.
questions.explanation: l_3 = l_0 x p_0 x p_1 x p_2 = 1,000 x 0.95 x 0.98 x 0.99 = 921.69. Option D subtracts the q's from 1 instead of multiplying the p's, Option B is l_2, and Option C multiplies the q's.

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: A life table has radix l_0 = 1,000, with q_0 = 0.05 and q_1 = 0.02. Calculate d_1, the number dying between exact ages 1 and 2, correct to 1 decimal place.
questions.explanation: First l_1 = 1,000 x 0.95 = 950, so d_1 = l_1 x q_1 = 950 x 0.02 = 19.0. Option C applies q_1 to the radix instead of l_1, Option A is d_0, and Option D is l_2.

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: The survival function of a population is s(x) = 1 - x/120 for 0 <= x <= 120, where s(x) = l_x / l_0. What is the probability that a newborn survives to age 30?
questions.explanation: The probability of surviving from birth to age 30 is s(30) = 1 - 30/120 = 0.75. Option D is the probability of dying before 30, while Options B and C come from using the wrong limiting age (150 and 100).

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: The survival function of a population is s(x) = 1 - x/120 for 0 <= x <= 120, where s(x) = l_x / l_0. Calculate 20p40, the probability that a life aged 40 survives to age 60, correct to 4 decimal places.
questions.explanation: 20p40 = s(60)/s(40) = (60/120)/(80/120) = 60/80 = 0.7500. Option C is s(60) alone (survival from birth), Option D is s(20), and Option A is 20q40.

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: The survival function of a population is s(x) = 1 - x/120 for 0 <= x <= 120, where s(x) = l_x / l_0. Calculate the probability that a newborn dies between ages 30 and 60, correct to 2 decimal places.
questions.explanation: P(newborn dies between 30 and 60) = s(30) - s(60) = 0.75 - 0.50 = 0.25. Option D is the probability for a life already aged 30 (it divides by s(30)), Option B is s(60), and Option C is s(30).

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: The survival function of a population is s(x) = 1 - x/120 for 0 <= x <= 120, where s(x) = l_x / l_0. If the life table is built with radix l_0 = 100,000, find l_48.
questions.explanation: l_48 = l_0 x s(48) = 100,000 x (1 - 48/120) = 60,000. Option B is the number who have died by age 48, Option A uses 100 as the limiting age, and Option D is l_49.

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: The survival function of a population is s(x) = (1 - x/100)^2 for 0 <= x <= 100, where s(x) = l_x / l_0. Calculate 20p30, the probability that a life aged 30 survives to age 50, correct to 4 decimal places.
questions.explanation: 20p30 = s(50)/s(30) = (0.5)^2/(0.7)^2 = 0.25/0.49 = 0.5102. Option D forgets to square, Option A is s(50) (survival from birth), and Option B is 20q30.

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: The survival function of a population is s(x) = (1 - x/100)^2 for 0 <= x <= 100, where s(x) = l_x / l_0. Calculate 20q50, the probability that a life aged 50 dies before age 70, correct to 2 decimal places.
questions.explanation: 20q50 = 1 - s(70)/s(50) = 1 - 0.09/0.25 = 0.64. Option B forgets the square, Option D is 20p50, and Option A is the unconditional probability for a newborn (it does not divide by s(50)).

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: The effective rate of interest is 6% per annum. Calculate the equivalent force of interest delta, correct to 5 decimal places.
questions.explanation: Since 1 + i = e^delta, delta = ln(1.06) = 0.05827. Option D is d = 0.06/1.06, Option B treats 6% as the force and finds the effective rate e^0.06 - 1, and Option C is the nominal rate i^(12).

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: The effective rate of discount is d = 5% per annum. Calculate the equivalent effective rate of interest i = d/(1-d), correct to 5 decimal places.
questions.explanation: i = d/(1-d) = 0.05/0.95 = 0.05263. Option D uses the formula for d in terms of i, Option A is v = 1 - d, and Option C is d(1+d), which is also wrong.

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: At an effective rate of interest of 10% per annum, calculate v^4, correct to 5 decimal places.
questions.explanation: v^4 = (1.1)^-4 = 1/1.4641 = 0.68301. Option B is the accumulation factor (1.1)^4, Option C uses simple discount 1 - 4i, and Option A is v^5.

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: A nominal rate of interest i^(4) = 8% per annum is convertible quarterly. Calculate the equivalent effective annual rate i, correct to 5 decimal places.
questions.explanation: 1 + i = (1 + i^(4)/4)^4 = (1.02)^4, so i = 0.08243. Option B treats the nominal rate as if it were effective, Option D finds a quarterly effective rate from 8% effective, and Option C compounds for 8 quarters.

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: The effective rate of interest is 12% per annum. Calculate the equivalent nominal rate i^(12), convertible monthly, correct to 5 decimal places.
questions.explanation: i^(12) = 12[(1.12)^(1/12) - 1] = 0.11387. Option D assumes i^(12) equals i, Option B is the monthly effective rate before multiplying by 12, and Option C goes the wrong way and treats 12% as the nominal rate.

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: The force of interest is delta = 0.07 per annum. Calculate the discount factor v, correct to 5 decimal places.
questions.explanation: Since v = e^(-delta), v = e^(-0.07) = 0.93239. Option D treats 7% as an effective rate (1/1.07), Option B is 1 + i = e^0.07, and Option A treats 0.07 as d.

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: At an effective rate of interest of 5% per annum, calculate a_4|, the present value of an annuity-certain of 1 per annum for 4 years with payments at the END of each year, correct to 4 decimal places.
questions.explanation: a_4| = (1 - v^4)/i = (1 - (1.05)^-4)/0.05 = 3.5460. Option B is the annuity-due value a-double-dot_4| = (1.05)a_4|, Option A is s_4|, the accumulated value, and Option C discounts all four payments from time 4.

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: At an effective rate of interest of 10% per annum, calculate s_3|, the accumulated value at time 3 of payments of 1 at the END of each year for 3 years, correct to 3 decimal places.
questions.explanation: s_3| = ((1.1)^3 - 1)/0.1 = 0.331/0.1 = 3.310. Option D is s-double-dot_3| for an annuity-due, Option C is the present value a_3|, and Option A accumulates every payment for the full 3 years.

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: At a certain rate of interest, a_9| = 7.1078 for payments made at the end of each year. Using a-double-dot_n| = 1 + a_(n-1)|, find a-double-dot_10|, the value of an annuity-due of 1 per annum for 10 years with payments at the BEGINNING of each year.
questions.explanation: An annuity-due of 10 payments is a payment of 1 now plus an annuity-immediate of the remaining 9, so a-double-dot_10| = 1 + 7.1078 = 8.1078. Option C forgets the payment at time 0, Option D subtracts it instead of adding it, and Option A wrongly scales a_9| up in proportion.

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: In a life table l_45 = 92,000 and q_45 = 0.0035. Calculate l_46, correct to 1 decimal place.
questions.explanation: l_46 = l_45 x p_45 = 92,000 x (1 - 0.0035) = 91,678.0. Option D is d_45, the number dying, Option C adds the deaths instead of subtracting them, and Option B subtracts the probability itself rather than the number of deaths.

questions.topic: Actuarial Symbols, Notations and Life Tables
questions.question: A life table gives: l_20 = 100,000; l_21 = 99,820; l_22 = 99,630; l_23 = 99,428; l_24 = 99,213; l_25 = 98,985. Calculate p_23, correct to 5 decimal places.
questions.explanation: p_23 = l_24 / l_23 = 99,213/99,428 = 0.99784. Option A is p_22, Option B is q_23, and Option D is 4p20, which divides by the radix.

questions.topic: Actuarial Science, Insurance and the Role of Actuaries
questions.question: Which of the following is among the most common industries or areas where actuaries work?
questions.explanation: Actuaries work across insurance (property and casualty as well as life and annuities) and in the employee benefits industry (retirement benefits), so every listed option is a common area. Choosing only A, B or C would leave out other areas that are equally typical, which is why All of the above is the best answer.

questions.topic: Actuarial Science, Insurance and the Role of Actuaries
questions.question: ________ offers several term and permanent insurance products to provide death benefit protection to its customers.
