questions.question: The principle that N100 received today is worth more than N100 received a year from now, because the money received today can be invested to earn interest, is called
questions.explanation: The time value of money is the idea that money available now is worth more than the same amount in the future because of its potential earning capacity. Option C refers to the stated face value of a security, not its value over time. Option D is a capital-budgeting measure that actually ignores the time value of money, and option B is one method of calculating present values.

questions.topic: Time Value of Money: Compound Interest and Discounting
questions.question: Why is a naira received today worth more than a naira received in the future, under the time value of money?

options.a: Because future payments are certain while present payments are not
options.b: Because money received now can be invested to earn interest
options.c: Because interest is charged only on loans and never paid on deposits
options.d: Because the face value of naira notes falls every year

questions.explanation: The time value of money rests on earning capacity: provided money can earn interest, any amount is worth more the sooner it is received. Option D confuses face value, which does not change, with value over time. Option A has certainty the wrong way round, and option C is simply false since deposits earn interest.

questions.topic: Time Value of Money: Compound Interest and Discounting
questions.question: Which of the following correctly describes simple interest at rate r per annum?

options.a: Interest is deducted in advance, so the value now of 1 due at time t is (1 - r)^t
options.b: Interest is added continuously, so 1 grows to e^(rt) after t years
options.c: Interest is earned on the principal and on interest already earned, so 1 grows to (1 + r)^t
options.d: Interest is earned only on the original principal, so 1 grows to 1 + rt after t years

questions.explanation: Simple interest is calculated on the original principal only, so a unit investment grows linearly to 1 + rt and in general A = P(1 + rt). Option C describes compound interest, where interest also earns interest. Option A describes compound discounting, and option B describes continuous compounding at force of interest r.

questions.topic: Time Value of Money: Compound Interest and Discounting
questions.question: A thrift cooperative in Ibadan credits interest to each member's savings at the end of every year, and the credited interest itself earns interest in the following years. This arrangement is an example of
questions.explanation: When interest is added to the balance and then earns interest itself, the account grows by compound interest, so P accumulates to P(1 + i)^n. Option A would pay interest on the original savings only. Options B and D describe interest deducted in advance, which is not what happens here.

questions.topic: Time Value of Money: Compound Interest and Discounting
questions.question: How does the growth of an investment under simple interest differ from its growth under compound interest at the same positive rate?

options.a: Both grow geometrically, but simple interest uses a lower rate
options.b: Simple interest grows geometrically, while compound interest grows linearly
options.c: Both grow linearly, but compound interest has a steeper line
options.d: Simple interest grows linearly (1 + rt), while compound interest grows geometrically ((1 + i)^t)

questions.explanation: Under simple interest the same amount of interest is added each year, so the value 1 + rt is a straight line in t, while under compound interest each year's growth is a fixed percentage of a rising balance, giving the geometric curve (1 + i)^t. Option B swaps the two, and options C and A wrongly give both methods the same shape.

questions.topic: Time Value of Money: Compound Interest and Discounting
questions.question: For the same positive annual rate r, how do the accumulated values of 1 under simple interest, 1 + rt, and compound interest, (1 + r)^t, compare at exactly t = 1 year?

options.a: It depends on whether r is above or below 10%
options.b: Simple interest gives more, because it is not reduced by compounding
options.c: They are equal, both being 1 + r
options.d: Compound interest gives more, because interest earns interest

questions.explanation: At t = 1, (1 + r)^1 = 1 + r x 1, so the two methods give exactly the same accumulation; compounding only makes a difference once interest has been credited and starts earning interest. Option D is true for t greater than 1, and option B is true for t less than 1. Option A is wrong because the equality at t = 1 holds for every rate.

questions.topic: Time Value of Money: Compound Interest and Discounting
questions.question: A trader in Yaba invests N25,000 at a simple interest rate of 9% per annum. What is the accumulated value at the end of 4 years, to the nearest naira?
questions.explanation: Under simple interest A = P(1 + rt) = 25,000(1 + 0.09 x 4) = 25,000 x 1.36 = N34,000. Option C compounds the interest as 25,000(1.09)^4, which is wrong because simple interest is earned on the principal only. Option D uses 3 years instead of 4, and option B is just the interest, not the accumulated value.

questions.topic: Time Value of Money: Compound Interest and Discounting
questions.question: Amaka deposits N40,000 in a savings scheme that pays simple interest at 12% per annum. How much interest does she earn in 9 months, to the nearest naira?
questions.explanation: Time must be in years, so t = 9/12 = 0.75 and interest = Prt = 40,000 x 0.12 x 0.75 = N3,600. Option D charges a full year's interest, option C wrongly writes 9 months as 0.9 of a year, and option A uses compound growth 40,000[(1.12)^0.75 - 1] instead of simple interest.

questions.topic: Time Value of Money: Compound Interest and Discounting
questions.question: A sum of N20,000 invested at simple interest grows to N26,000 after 5 years. What is the annual rate of simple interest?
questions.explanation: From A = P(1 + rt): 26,000 = 20,000(1 + 5r), so 1 + 5r = 1.3 and r = 0.3/5 = 6.00%. Option B solves (1 + r)^5 = 1.3, which is the compound interest rate, not the simple rate. Option D is the total growth over 5 years without dividing by the time, and option A wrongly divides the interest by the final amount instead of the principal.

questions.topic: Time Value of Money: Compound Interest and Discounting
questions.question: How long will it take N15,000 to grow to N21,000 at a simple interest rate of 8% per annum?
questions.explanation: Simple interest gives 21,000 = 15,000(1 + 0.08t), so 0.08t = 0.4 and t = 0.4/0.08 = 5.00 years. Option D solves (1.08)^t = 1.4, which assumes compound interest. Options C and A mix up which amount goes in the numerator and denominator.

questions.topic: Time Value of Money: Compound Interest and Discounting
questions.question: A company must pay a debt of N50,000 in 3 years' time and can invest money now at a simple interest rate of 10% per annum. How much must it invest now (to 2 decimal places)?
questions.explanation: Rearranging A = P(1 + rt) gives P = A/(1 + rt) = 50,000/(1 + 0.10 x 3) = 50,000/1.3 = N38,461.54. Option A treats 10% as a simple discount rate, 50,000(1 - 0.3). Option B discounts at compound interest, 50,000/(1.1)^3, and option C discounts for only one year.

questions.topic: Time Value of Money: Compound Interest and Discounting
questions.question: Under a rate of simple discount d per annum, the value now, P, of an amount A payable at time t years is
questions.explanation: Simple discount deducts d per year of the amount due, in proportion to time, so P = A(1 - dt). Option C is present value under simple interest, and option A is compound discounting at an effective discount rate. Option D is an accumulation, not a present value.

questions.topic: Time Value of Money: Compound Interest and Discounting
questions.question: A bill of N60,000 is payable in 2 years. Using a rate of simple discount of 7% per annum, what is its present value (to 2 decimal places)?
questions.explanation: At simple discount the present value is P = A(1 - dt) = 60,000(1 - 0.07 x 2) = 60,000 x 0.86 = N51,600.00. Option C treats 7% as simple interest, 60,000/1.14, and option D applies the discount in compound form, 60,000(0.93)^2. Option B discounts for only one year.

questions.topic: Time Value of Money: Compound Interest and Discounting
questions.question: An amount of N2,000 is invested for 3 years at a rate of simple discount of 6% per annum. To what amount does it accumulate at the end of the 3 years (to 2 decimal places)?
questions.explanation: Under simple discount P = A(1 - dt), so the accumulated value is A = P/(1 - dt) = 2,000/(1 - 0.06 x 3) = 2,000/0.82 = N2,439.02. Option A treats 6% as simple interest, 2,000 x 1.18. Option B multiplies by (1 - dt) instead of dividing, which gives a present value, and option D uses the compound form 2,000/(0.94)^3.

questions.topic: Time Value of Money: Compound Interest and Discounting
questions.question: To 4 decimal places, to what amount does N1 accumulate in one year at a rate of simple discount of 5% per annum?
questions.explanation: A unit invested for one period at simple discount d accumulates to 1/(1 - d) = 1/0.95 = 1.0526. Option B treats 5% as an interest rate, giving 1.05. Option A is 1 - d, which is the present value of 1 due in a year, not an accumulation.

questions.topic: Time Value of Money: Compound Interest and Discounting
questions.question: Under compound interest at an effective rate i per period, what does the expression (1 + i)^n measure?

options.a: The effective rate of discount over n periods
options.b: The accumulated value at time n of 1 invested at time 0
options.c: The present value at time 0 of 1 due at time n
options.d: The total interest earned on 1 over n periods

questions.explanation: (1 + i)^n is the accumulation factor: it tells you what a unit investment grows to after n periods, so P grows to P(1 + i)^n. Option C describes the discount factor v^n = (1 + i)^-n, the reverse operation. Option D is (1 + i)^n - 1, which excludes the original unit.

questions.topic: Time Value of Money: Compound Interest and Discounting
questions.question: N80,000 is invested at an effective rate of compound interest of 7% per annum. What is the accumulated value after 6 years, to the nearest naira?
questions.explanation: The accumulated value is P(1 + i)^n = 80,000(1.07)^6 = N120,058. Option B uses simple interest, 80,000(1 + 0.07 x 6). Option D accumulates for only 5 years, and option A discounts instead of accumulating.

questions.topic: Time Value of Money: Compound Interest and Discounting
questions.question: A cooperative society invests N50,000 at an effective compound interest rate of 10% per annum for 3 years. How much interest does it earn over the 3 years, to the nearest naira?
questions.explanation: Compound interest earned is P[(1 + i)^n - 1] = 50,000[(1.1)^3 - 1] = 50,000 x 0.331 = N16,550. Option B is the simple interest 50,000 x 0.1 x 3, which ignores interest on interest. Option C is the full accumulated value rather than the interest, and option A uses only 2 years.

questions.topic: Time Value of Money: Compound Interest and Discounting
questions.question: What is the present value of N500,000 due in 5 years at an effective rate of compound interest of 8% per annum, to the nearest naira?
questions.explanation: Present value = A(1 + i)^-n = 500,000(1.08)^-5 = N340,292. Option C discounts at simple interest, 500,000/(1 + 0.4), and option A uses simple discount, 500,000(1 - 0.4). Option D wrongly takes the discount factor as 1 - i = 0.92 instead of 1/1.08.

questions.topic: Time Value of Money: Compound Interest and Discounting
questions.question: At an effective rate of interest of 6% per annum, what is the value of the discount factor v^10, to 4 decimal places?
questions.explanation: v = (1.06)^-1, so v^10 = (1.06)^-10 = 0.5584, the present value of 1 due in 10 years. Option A is the accumulation factor (1.06)^10, the reverse operation. Option D wrongly uses 0.94 for v, and option C is the simple-discount style value 1 - 10(0.06).

questions.topic: Time Value of Money: Compound Interest and Discounting
questions.question: N100,000 is invested for 2 years at 10% per annum. By how much does the interest earned at compound interest (compounded annually) exceed the interest earned at simple interest?
questions.explanation: Compound interest = 100,000[(1.1)^2 - 1] = N21,000 and simple interest = 100,000 x 0.1 x 2 = N20,000, so the difference is N1,000, which is interest earned on the first year's interest. Options D and C are the two interest amounts themselves, not their difference, and option A is one year's interest.

questions.topic: Time Value of Money: Compound Interest and Discounting
questions.question: An investment of N10,000 grows to N14,641 in 4 years under compound interest. What is the effective annual rate of interest?
questions.explanation: Solve 10,000(1 + i)^4 = 14,641, so 1 + i = (1.4641)^(1/4) = 1.1 and i = 10.00%. Option B averages the growth as if it were simple interest (46.41%/4), and option C is the total growth over 4 years. Option D is 1 - (1.4641)^(-1/4), which is the equivalent rate of discount d, not i.

questions.topic: Time Value of Money: Compound Interest and Discounting
questions.question: How long does it take a sum of money to double at an effective compound interest rate of 9% per annum (to 2 decimal places)?
questions.explanation: Solve (1.09)^n = 2, giving n = ln 2/ln 1.09 = 8.04 years. Option D is the doubling time under simple interest (1/0.09), and option A divides ln 2 by 0.09 as if 9% were the force of interest. Option C wrongly divides 2 by the rate.

questions.topic: Time Value of Money: Compound Interest and Discounting
questions.question: How long will it take N30,000 to accumulate to N45,000 at an effective compound interest rate of 6% per annum (to 2 decimal places)?
questions.explanation: Solve 30,000(1.06)^n = 45,000, so (1.06)^n = 1.5 and n = ln 1.5/ln 1.06 = 6.96 years. Option A is the simple interest answer 0.5/0.06, and option D divides ln 1.5 by 0.06, treating 6% as a force of interest. Option C divides the ratio by the rate.

questions.topic: Time Value of Money: Compound Interest and Discounting
questions.question: A Lagos fintech fund turns N50,000 into N80,000 over 6 years with interest compounded annually. What effective annual rate of interest did it earn (to 2 decimal places)?
questions.explanation: Solve 50,000(1 + i)^6 = 80,000, so i = (1.6)^(1/6) - 1 = 8.15%. Option A is the simple interest rate 60%/6. Option C is ln 1.6/6, which is the force of interest, not the effective rate, and option B uses 5 years instead of 6.

questions.topic: Time Value of Money: Compound Interest and Discounting
questions.question: A sum of money amounts to N24,200 in 2 years at an effective compound interest rate of 10% per annum. What was the original sum (to 2 decimal places)?
questions.explanation: The principal is 24,200(1.1)^-2 = 24,200/1.21 = N20,000.00. Option A discounts at simple interest, 24,200/1.2. Option B subtracts 20% of the final amount, and option D discounts for only one year.

questions.topic: Time Value of Money: Compound Interest and Discounting
questions.question: A payment of N300,000 is due at the end of year 7. Using an effective rate of interest of 5% per annum, what is its value at the end of year 2, to the nearest naira?
questions.explanation: Moving a payment back from time 7 to time 2 means discounting for 5 years: 300,000 v^5 = 300,000(1.05)^-5 = N235,058. Option C discounts all the way to time 0 (7 years), and option A discounts for only 2 years. Option D adds the two times together and discounts for 9 years.

questions.topic: Time Value of Money: Compound Interest and Discounting
questions.question: N10,000 is invested for 2 years and 6 months at an effective compound interest rate of 12% per annum. What is the accumulated value (to 2 decimal places)?
questions.explanation: Compound interest works for non-integer time, so A = 10,000(1.12)^2.5 = N13,275.32. Option D uses simple interest, option B ignores the extra 6 months, and option A wrongly treats 12% as a nominal rate convertible half-yearly, 10,000(1.06)^5.

questions.topic: Time Value of Money: Compound Interest and Discounting
questions.question: At an effective rate of interest i per annum, what does v^n = (1 + i)^-n represent?

options.a: The interest earned in the nth year on 1 invested now
options.b: The accumulated value after n years of 1 invested now
options.c: The nominal rate of interest convertible n times a year
options.d: The present value of 1 due at the end of n years

questions.explanation: v = (1 + i)^-1 is the present value of a unit payment due in one period, so v^n is the present value of 1 due in n periods; multiplying by v^n is how we discount. Option B is the accumulation factor (1 + i)^n. Option C confuses a rate convertible n times a year with a discount factor.

questions.topic: Time Value of Money: Compound Interest and Discounting
questions.question: Under compound interest at an effective rate i per annum, to find the value at time 3 of a payment due at time 7 you should multiply the payment by
questions.explanation: The payment is moved 4 years earlier, from time 7 back to time 3, so it is discounted by v^4 = (1 + i)^-4. Option C would move it 4 years later instead. Option D discounts all the way to time 0, and option A uses the wrong number of years.

questions.topic: Time Value of Money: Compound Interest and Discounting
questions.question: A pension fund in Abuja values two liabilities of N1,000,000 each, one due in 10 years and one due in 20 years, at the same positive effective rate of interest. Which statement is correct?

options.a: The liability due in 20 years has the larger present value, because it accumulates more interest
options.b: Both liabilities have the same present value, because the amounts are equal
options.c: The liability due in 10 years has the smaller present value, because it is paid sooner
options.d: The liability due in 20 years has the smaller present value, because v^n falls as n increases

questions.explanation: The present value of 1,000,000 due at time n is 1,000,000v^n, and since 0 < v < 1 the factor v^n gets smaller as n grows, so the later liability is worth less today. Option B ignores the time value of money, while options A and C confuse discounting with accumulation.

questions.topic: Time Value of Money: Compound Interest and Discounting
questions.question: The effective rate of discount d per annum is best described as

options.a: the discount on 1 due a year hence, i.e. interest for the year paid at the start of the year
options.b: the interest on 1 for a year, paid at the end of the year
options.c: the instantaneous rate of growth of a fund under continuous compounding
options.d: the annual rate of interest convertible m times a year

questions.explanation: In international actuarial notation d is the discount on 1 due a year hence: the year's interest charged at the start, so d = 1 - v = i/(1 + i). Option B describes the effective rate of interest i. Option D describes a nominal rate i^(m), and option C describes the force of interest delta.

questions.topic: Time Value of Money: Compound Interest and Discounting
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a correct expression for the effective rate of discount d in terms of the effective rate of interest i (with v = 1/(1 + i))?
questions.explanation: The discount on 1 due a year hence is 1 - v, and since 1 - 1/(1 + i) = i/(1 + i) = iv, options C, D and B are all the same correct quantity. The expression i/(1 - i) is wrong; it would make d larger than i, whereas d is always smaller than i when i > 0.

questions.topic: Time Value of Money: Compound Interest and Discounting
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a correct expression for the discount factor v?
questions.explanation: The discount factor is the present value of 1 due in a year, so v = (1 + i)^-1, which equals 1 - d because d is the discount on that unit, and equals e^-delta because 1 + i = e^delta. Options C, B and A are therefore all correct. 1 + d is greater than 1, so it cannot be a present value of 1 due in the future.

questions.topic: Time Value of Money: Compound Interest and Discounting
questions.question: The effective rate of interest is 8% per annum. What is the equivalent effective rate of discount d per annum (to 2 decimal places)?
questions.explanation: d = i/(1 + i) = 0.08/1.08 = 7.41%, the interest on 1 for a year when it is paid at the start of the year. Option C uses i/(1 - i), which is the wrong way round. Option B is ln 1.08, the force of interest, and option A is v = 1/1.08, the discount factor rather than the discount rate.

questions.topic: Time Value of Money: Compound Interest and Discounting
questions.question: The effective rate of discount is 6% per annum. What is the equivalent effective rate of interest i per annum (to 2 decimal places)?
questions.explanation: Since v = 1 - d = 0.94 and 1 + i = 1/v, i = d/(1 - d) = 0.06/0.94 = 6.38%. Option A uses d/(1 + d), which converts in the wrong direction, and option B assumes i equals d. Option D is e^0.06 - 1, which treats 6% as a force of interest.

questions.topic: Time Value of Money: Compound Interest and Discounting
questions.question: What is the present value of N200,000 due in 3 years at an effective rate of discount of 5% per annum (to 2 decimal places)?
questions.explanation: With an effective discount rate, v = 1 - d = 0.95, so the present value is 200,000(0.95)^3 = N171,475.00. Option D treats 5% as an interest rate, 200,000/(1.05)^3. Option A uses simple discount 200,000(1 - 0.15), and option C discounts for only 2 years.

questions.topic: Time Value of Money: Compound Interest and Discounting
questions.question: A bill of exchange for N100,000 is due in one year. If the effective rate of interest is 12% per annum, what is the amount of discount on the bill, i.e. the difference between its face value and its present value (to 2 decimal places)?
questions.explanation: The discount on 1 due a year hence is d = i/(1 + i) = 0.12/1.12, so the discount is 100,000 x 0.12/1.12 = N10,714.29. Option C is the interest 12% of face value, which is paid at the end, not deducted at the start. Option D is the present value of the bill itself, and option A uses i/(1 - i).

questions.topic: Time Value of Money: Compound Interest and Discounting
questions.question: An insurer must pay N1,000,000 in 4 years. Using an effective rate of discount of 10% per annum, what is the present value of the payment (to 2 decimal places)?
questions.explanation: Here v = 1 - d = 0.9, so present value = 1,000,000(0.9)^4 = N656,100.00. Option A treats 10% as an interest rate, 1,000,000/(1.1)^4. Option C applies simple discount for 4 years, and option B discounts for only 3 years.

questions.topic: Time Value of Money: Compound Interest and Discounting
questions.question: A Nigerian bank advertises a savings rate of 24% per annum convertible monthly. Which statement about this rate is correct?

options.a: It is a force of interest of 24%, so N100 grows to 100e^0.24 in a year
options.b: It is a nominal rate of discount d^(12) = 24%, deducted at the start of each month
options.c: It is an effective annual rate, so N100 grows to exactly N124 in a year
options.d: It is a nominal rate i^(12) = 24%, so the effective rate per month is 2%

questions.explanation: A rate quoted 'convertible monthly' is a nominal rate i^(12); dividing by 12 gives the effective monthly rate of 2%, and a unit grows to (1 + 0.24/12)^12 in a year. Option C ignores the monthly conversion, which makes the effective annual rate higher than 24%. Option A describes continuous compounding, and option B describes a discount rate, not an interest rate.

questions.topic: Time Value of Money: Compound Interest and Discounting
questions.question: Two interest rates (for example a nominal rate convertible quarterly and an effective annual rate) are said to be equivalent when

options.a: they produce the same accumulated value from the same principal over the same period
options.b: they are quoted by the same bank for the same product
options.c: they have the same numerical value
options.d: they are both expressed per annum

questions.explanation: Equivalent rates describe the same growth: for example i^(m) and i are equivalent when (1 + i^(m)/m)^m = 1 + i, so one naira grows to the same amount over a year under either. Option C is wrong because equivalent rates usually have different numbers, such as 10% effective and 9.569% convertible monthly. Options B and D say nothing about growth.

questions.topic: Time Value of Money: Compound Interest and Discounting
questions.question: A bank quotes a nominal rate of interest of 12% per annum convertible quarterly, i^(4) = 12%. What is the equivalent effective annual rate of interest (to 2 decimal places)?
questions.explanation: The quarterly effective rate is i^(4)/4 = 3%, so 1 + i = (1.03)^4 and i = 12.55%. Option D wrongly takes the nominal rate as the effective rate. Option A compounds 6% twice, as if interest were convertible half-yearly, and option B is e^0.12 - 1, which treats 12% as a force of interest.

questions.topic: Time Value of Money: Compound Interest and Discounting
questions.question: A microfinance bank charges a nominal rate of interest of 18% per annum convertible monthly. What is the equivalent effective annual rate of interest (to 2 decimal places)?
questions.explanation: The monthly effective rate is 18%/12 = 1.5%, so i = (1.015)^12 - 1 = 19.56%. Option A ignores the monthly compounding. Option D compounds quarterly at 4.5% instead of monthly, and option B is continuous compounding e^0.18 - 1.

questions.topic: Time Value of Money: Compound Interest and Discounting
questions.question: The effective rate of interest is 21% per annum. What is the equivalent nominal rate of interest per annum convertible half-yearly, i^(2) (to 2 decimal places)?
questions.explanation: Set (1 + i^(2)/2)^2 = 1.21, so i^(2)/2 = (1.21)^(1/2) - 1 = 0.10 and i^(2) = 20.00%. Option A is the effective rate per half-year, which must be multiplied by 2 to give the nominal annual rate. Option C assumes nominal and effective rates are equal, and option B is ln 1.21, the force of interest.

questions.topic: Time Value of Money: Compound Interest and Discounting
questions.question: The effective rate of interest is 15% per annum. What is the equivalent nominal rate of interest convertible monthly, i^(12) (to 2 decimal places)?
questions.explanation: i^(12) = 12[(1.15)^(1/12) - 1] = 14.06%. Option A is the monthly effective rate (1.15)^(1/12) - 1, which has not been multiplied by 12. Option C is ln 1.15, the force of interest, which is the limit as m grows without bound, and option D ignores the conversion entirely.

questions.topic: Time Value of Money: Compound Interest and Discounting
questions.question: N200,000 is invested for 3 years at a nominal rate of interest of 8% per annum convertible quarterly. What is the accumulated value, to the nearest naira?
questions.explanation: With i^(4) = 8%, the quarterly rate is 2% and there are 12 quarters, so A = 200,000(1.02)^12 = N253,648. Option B treats 8% as an effective annual rate, 200,000(1.08)^3, and option D uses simple interest. Option C compounds continuously, 200,000e^0.24.

questions.topic: Time Value of Money: Compound Interest and Discounting
questions.question: N50,000 is deposited for 18 months at a nominal rate of interest of 12% per annum convertible monthly. What is the accumulated value (to 2 decimal places)?
questions.explanation: The monthly rate is 12%/12 = 1% over 18 months, so A = 50,000(1.01)^18 = N59,807.37. Option B treats 12% as effective annual, 50,000(1.12)^1.5. Option D uses simple interest, and option C counts only 12 months.

questions.topic: Time Value of Money: Compound Interest and Discounting
questions.question: What is the present value of N1,000,000 due in 2 years at a nominal rate of interest of 10% per annum convertible half-yearly, to the nearest naira?
questions.explanation: The half-yearly rate is 5% for 4 half-years, so PV = 1,000,000(1.05)^-4 = N822,702. Option D treats 10% as an effective annual rate, and option A uses only 2 half-years. Option B wrongly takes the discount factor per half-year as 0.95 instead of 1/1.05.

questions.topic: Time Value of Money: Compound Interest and Discounting
questions.question: The effective rate of interest is 12% per annum. What is the equivalent effective rate of interest per month (to 2 decimal places)?
questions.explanation: Equivalent rates give the same growth over a year, so (1 + j)^12 = 1.12 and j = (1.12)^(1/12) - 1 = 0.95% per month. Option B simply divides 12% by 12, which would give more than 12% a year once compounded. Options C and D are the equivalent quarterly and half-yearly rates, not the monthly rate.

questions.topic: Time Value of Money: Compound Interest and Discounting
questions.question: A savings account earns an effective rate of 1% per month. What is the equivalent effective rate of interest per quarter (to 2 decimal places)?
questions.explanation: A quarter has 3 months, so the quarterly rate is (1.01)^3 - 1 = 3.03%. Option A adds the three monthly rates and ignores interest on interest. Option C is the annual rate (1.01)^12 - 1, and option D compounds for 4 months instead of 3.

questions.topic: Time Value of Money: Compound Interest and Discounting
questions.question: A nominal rate of interest of 8% per annum is convertible quarterly. What is the equivalent nominal rate of interest per annum convertible half-yearly, i^(2) (to 2 decimal places)?
questions.explanation: The quarterly rate is 2%, so the half-yearly rate is (1.02)^2 - 1 = 4.04% and i^(2) = 2 x 4.04% = 8.08%. Option C assumes nominal rates with different conversion frequencies are equal. Option B is the effective annual rate (1.02)^4 - 1, and option D is the half-yearly rate that has not been multiplied by 2.

questions.topic: Time Value of Money: Compound Interest and Discounting
questions.question: Bank A offers 12% per annum convertible monthly and Bank B offers an effective rate of 12.5% per annum. Which bank gives the higher return on a one-year deposit, and why?

options.a: Bank B, because 12.5% is higher than 12%
options.b: Neither, because both rates are equivalent effective annual rates
options.c: Bank B, because Bank A's effective annual rate is exactly 12.00%
options.d: Bank A, because its effective annual rate is about 12.68%

questions.explanation: Rates with different conversion frequencies must be compared as effective annual rates: Bank A gives (1 + 0.12/12)^12 - 1 = (1.01)^12 - 1 = 12.68%, which beats Bank B's 12.5%. Options A and C compare a nominal rate directly with an effective rate, forgetting that monthly conversion adds interest on interest. Option B is wrong because the two rates are not equivalent.

questions.topic: Time Value of Money: Compound Interest and Discounting
questions.question: A bill of N500,000 is due in one year. Using a nominal rate of discount of 8% per annum convertible half-yearly, d^(2) = 8%, what is its present value, to the nearest naira?
questions.explanation: With d^(2) = 8%, the discount per half-year is 4%, so PV = 500,000(1 - 0.04)^2 = 500,000 x 0.9216 = N460,800. Option B treats 8% as an effective annual discount rate, option A treats it as a nominal interest rate i^(2), and option C discounts for only one half-year.

questions.topic: Time Value of Money: Compound Interest and Discounting
questions.question: The nominal rate of discount is 12% per annum convertible quarterly, d^(4) = 12%. What is the equivalent effective annual rate of discount d (to 2 decimal places)?
questions.explanation: The quarterly discount rate is 3%, so 1 - d = (1 - 0.03)^4 = 0.8853 and d = 11.47%. Option D wrongly takes the nominal rate as the effective rate. Option C treats 12% as a nominal interest rate i^(4) and finds the effective interest rate, and option B is 1 - e^-0.12, which treats 12% as a force of interest.

questions.topic: Time Value of Money: Compound Interest and Discounting
questions.question: The force of interest delta is best defined as

options.a: the effective rate of interest earned over one complete year
options.b: the nominal rate of interest convertible twelve times a year
options.c: the limit of the nominal rate i^(m) as m tends to infinity, i.e. the instantaneous rate of growth
options.d: the interest on 1 for a year paid at the start of the year

questions.explanation: The force of interest is the instantaneous rate of growth of a fund, like a nominal rate compounded continuously, so delta = lim i^(m) as m tends to infinity and 1 + i = e^delta. Option A is the effective rate i, option D is the rate of discount d, and option B is i^(12).

questions.topic: Time Value of Money: Compound Interest and Discounting
questions.question: For a given positive effective annual rate of interest i, which ordering of the equivalent rates is correct?
questions.explanation: To produce the same effective rate i, a rate that is converted more often needs a smaller nominal value, so i^(m) falls as m rises and the force of interest, the limit as m grows without bound, is the smallest; for i = 10%, i^(2) = 9.762%, i^(12) = 9.569% and delta = 9.531%. Option B reverses the order, and option C wrongly treats equivalent rates as numerically equal.

questions.topic: Time Value of Money: Compound Interest and Discounting
questions.question: A nominal rate of interest is fixed at 10% per annum. As the number of conversions per year m increases (m = 1, 2, 4, 12, ...), the equivalent effective annual rate of interest

options.b: increases without limit as m grows
options.d: stays at 10% for every value of m

questions.explanation: The effective rate (1 + 0.1/m)^m - 1 rises with m, from 10% at m = 1 to 10.25% at m = 2 and 10.471% at m = 12, but it is bounded by continuous compounding at e^0.1 - 1 = 10.52%. Option A describes what happens to the equivalent nominal rate when the effective rate is fixed instead. Option B is wrong because the growth levels off at the continuous limit.

questions.topic: Time Value of Money: Compound Interest and Discounting
questions.question: Which of the following relationships involving the force of interest delta is NOT correct?
questions.explanation: Because the limit of (1 + i^(m)/m)^m is e^delta, we get 1 + i = e^delta, which can be written delta = ln(1 + i), and taking reciprocals gives v = e^-delta; options A, C and D are all correct. The expression e^i - 1 mixes up the roles of i and delta; the correct direction is i = e^delta - 1.

questions.topic: Time Value of Money: Compound Interest and Discounting
questions.question: In international actuarial notation, the Greek letter delta denotes
questions.explanation: Delta is the force of interest, the instantaneous rate of growth under continuous compounding, linked to the effective rate by 1 + i = e^delta. Option B is denoted d, option C is denoted d^(m), and option D is denoted by the Greek letter mu.

questions.topic: Time Value of Money: Compound Interest and Discounting
questions.question: What is the force of interest delta per annum equivalent to an effective rate of interest of 8% per annum (to 4 decimal places)?
questions.explanation: Since 1 + i = e^delta, delta = ln(1.08) = 0.0770. Option D assumes delta equals i, but the force of interest is always a little less than i when i > 0. Option B is the rate of discount d = i/(1 + i), and option C is e^0.08 - 1, which applies the formula in the wrong direction.

questions.topic: Time Value of Money: Compound Interest and Discounting
questions.question: The force of interest is 6% per annum. What is the equivalent effective annual rate of interest (to 2 decimal places)?
questions.explanation: From 1 + i = e^delta, i = e^0.06 - 1 = 6.18%. Option C assumes i equals delta, which ignores continuous compounding. Option D is ln 1.06, which converts in the wrong direction, and option B treats 6% as a discount rate.

questions.topic: Time Value of Money: Compound Interest and Discounting
questions.question: N250,000 is invested for 4 years at a constant force of interest of 9% per annum. What is the accumulated value, to the nearest naira?
questions.explanation: With a constant force of interest A = P e^(delta t) = 250,000 e^(0.09 x 4) = 250,000 e^0.36 = N358,332. Option D treats 9% as an effective annual rate, 250,000(1.09)^4. Option B uses simple interest, and option C accumulates for only 3 years.

questions.topic: Time Value of Money: Compound Interest and Discounting
questions.question: What is the present value of N1,000,000 due in 5 years at a constant force of interest of 10% per annum, to the nearest naira?
questions.explanation: With v = e^-delta, the present value is 1,000,000 e^(-0.1 x 5) = 1,000,000 e^-0.5 = N606,531. Option D treats 10% as an effective rate, 1,000,000(1.1)^-5. Options C and A use simple discount and simple interest respectively.

questions.topic: Time Value of Money: Compound Interest and Discounting
questions.question: What is the force of interest delta per annum equivalent to a nominal rate of interest of 8% per annum convertible quarterly (to 4 decimal places)?
questions.explanation: Since (1 + i^(4)/4)^4 = e^delta, delta = 4 ln(1.02) = 0.0792. Option B assumes delta equals the nominal rate, and option D is ln(1.02), the force for one quarter that has not been converted to an annual figure. Option C is the effective annual rate (1.02)^4 - 1, not the force of interest.

questions.topic: Time Value of Money: Compound Interest and Discounting
questions.question: An investment earns an effective rate of interest of 5% per quarter. What is the equivalent force of interest delta per annum (to 4 decimal places)?
questions.explanation: One year is 4 quarters, so e^delta = (1.05)^4 and delta = 4 ln(1.05) = 0.1952 per annum. Option D is the force per quarter, ln 1.05, not per annum. Option C multiplies 5% by 4, and option B is the effective annual rate (1.05)^4 - 1.

questions.topic: Time Value of Money: Compound Interest and Discounting
questions.question: How long does it take a sum of money to double at a constant force of interest of 7% per annum (to 2 decimal places)?
questions.explanation: Solve e^(0.07t) = 2, so t = ln 2/0.07 = 9.90 years. Option D is the simple interest doubling time 1/0.07. Option B is ln 2/ln 1.07, which treats 7% as an effective annual rate, and option C wrongly divides 2 by the rate.

questions.topic: Time Value of Money: Compound Interest and Discounting
questions.question: The force of interest is 5% per annum. What is the annual discount factor v (to 4 decimal places)?
questions.explanation: Since v = e^-delta, v = e^-0.05 = 0.9512. Option A is 1/1.05, which treats 5% as an effective rate of interest. Option D is 1 - 0.05, which treats it as an effective rate of discount, and option C is e^0.05, the accumulation factor.

questions.topic: Time Value of Money: Compound Interest and Discounting
questions.question: The force of interest is 10% per annum. What is the equivalent effective annual rate of discount d (to 2 decimal places)?
questions.explanation: Since v = e^-delta and d = 1 - v, d = 1 - e^-0.1 = 9.52%. Option B assumes d equals delta, and option C is e^0.1 - 1, which is the effective rate of interest i, not d. Option D treats 10% as an effective interest rate and computes 0.1/1.1.

questions.topic: Time Value of Money: Compound Interest and Discounting
questions.question: A bank pays interest at 15% per annum compounded continuously. What does a deposit of N40,000 accumulate to after 2 years (to 2 decimal places)?
questions.explanation: Continuous compounding at 15% means a force of interest delta = 0.15, so A = 40,000 e^(0.15 x 2) = 40,000 e^0.3 = N53,994.35. Option A compounds annually, 40,000(1.15)^2, which gives less than continuous compounding. Option C uses simple interest, and option B accumulates for only one year.

questions.topic: Time Value of Money: Compound Interest and Discounting
questions.question: The force of interest is 12% per annum. What is the equivalent nominal rate of interest per annum convertible monthly, i^(12) (to 2 decimal places)?
questions.explanation: Set (1 + i^(12)/12)^12 = e^0.12, so i^(12) = 12(e^0.01 - 1) = 12.06%. Option A assumes i^(12) equals delta, but i^(12) must be slightly larger than delta. Option B is the effective annual rate e^0.12 - 1, and option D wrongly treats 12% as the effective annual rate before converting to monthly.

questions.topic: Time Value of Money: Compound Interest and Discounting
questions.question: A single sum is invested for 6 years at 5% for 3 years and then 7% for 3 years, compared with 7% for 3 years and then 5% for 3 years. Which statement is correct?

options.a: The first order gives more, because the higher rate is applied to a larger balance
options.b: The final amounts are equal, because the accumulation factors (1.05)^3 and (1.07)^3 are simply multiplied
options.c: The final amounts cannot be compared without knowing the principal
options.d: The second order gives more, because the higher rate is earned first

questions.explanation: For one payment, the accumulation over consecutive periods is the product of the factors, (1.05)^3(1.07)^3, and multiplication does not depend on order. The order of rates matters only when further payments are made part-way, as with a second deposit at time 3. Options A and D wrongly assume order matters for a single sum, and option C fails because the principal scales both results equally.

questions.topic: Time Value of Money: Compound Interest and Discounting
questions.question: N100,000 is invested for 5 years. The effective rate of interest is 6% per annum for the first 2 years and 9% per annum for the next 3 years. What is the accumulated value at the end of 5 years, to the nearest naira?
questions.explanation: With changing rates the accumulation factors for consecutive periods are multiplied: 100,000(1.06)^2(1.09)^3 = N145,509. Option D uses the simple average rate 7.5% for all 5 years, which is not equivalent. Option C applies 6% for 3 years and 9% for 2 years, swapping the periods, and option A adds the interest as if it were simple.

questions.topic: Time Value of Money: Compound Interest and Discounting
questions.question: A payment of N500,000 is due at the end of year 4. The effective rate of interest is 10% per annum for years 1 and 2 and 12% per annum for years 3 and 4. What is the present value of the payment at time 0, to the nearest naira?
questions.explanation: Discount through each period at its own rate: PV = 500,000/[(1.1)^2(1.12)^2] = 500,000/1.517824 = N329,419. Options B and D use only one of the two rates for all 4 years. Option A wrongly uses 1 - i as the discount factor in each year.

questions.topic: Time Value of Money: Compound Interest and Discounting
questions.question: Investments of N50,000 now and a further N50,000 two years from now are accumulated to the end of year 5. The effective rate of interest is 8% per annum for the first 2 years and 10% per annum thereafter. What is the total accumulation at the end of year 5, to the nearest naira?
questions.explanation: The first deposit grows to 50,000(1.08)^2 = 58,320 at time 2; adding the second deposit gives 108,320, which then grows at 10% for 3 years: 108,320(1.1)^3 = N144,174. Option D forgets that the second N50,000 also earns interest for 3 years. Options A and B apply a single rate (10% or 8%) to the whole term instead of switching rates at time 2.

questions.topic: Time Value of Money: Compound Interest and Discounting
questions.question: In setting up an equation of value for payments made at different dates under compound interest, which statement is correct?

options.a: Payments can be added directly at their face values, whatever their dates
options.b: The comparison date must always be time 0, otherwise the answer changes
options.c: All payments must be valued at the same date, and any comparison date gives the same solution
options.d: Only payments made after the comparison date need to be adjusted for interest

questions.explanation: Money at different dates can only be compared after moving every payment to one common date, accumulating earlier payments and discounting later ones. Under compound interest, moving the whole equation to another date multiplies both sides by the same factor (1 + i)^k, so the solution does not change. Option A ignores the time value of money, and option B is wrong because time 0 is only a convenient choice.

questions.topic: Time Value of Money: Compound Interest and Discounting
questions.question: Tunde borrows N200,000 now at an effective rate of interest of 10% per annum. He repays N100,000 at the end of year 1 and clears the loan with a single payment at the end of year 3. What is the final payment?
questions.explanation: The equation of value at time 3 is 200,000(1.1)^3 = 100,000(1.1)^2 + X, so X = 266,200 - 121,000 = N145,200. Option B forgets to accumulate the N100,000 repayment from time 1 to time 3. Option A subtracts the repayment without allowing for its timing, and option C uses simple interest.

questions.topic: Time Value of Money: Compound Interest and Discounting
questions.question: Using an effective rate of interest of 9% per annum, what is the present value of N60,000 due in 2 years plus N80,000 due in 5 years, to the nearest naira?
questions.explanation: Discount each payment from its own date: 60,000(1.09)^-2 + 80,000(1.09)^-5 = 50,501 + 51,994 = N102,495. Option D discounts the combined N140,000 for 5 years, ignoring that N60,000 is paid earlier. Option B discounts the second payment for 3 years instead of 5, and option A uses 0.91 instead of 1/1.09 as the discount factor.

questions.topic: Time Value of Money: Compound Interest and Discounting
questions.question: Using an effective rate of interest of 7% per annum, what is the accumulated value at the end of year 4 of N30,000 paid now and N40,000 paid at the end of year 2, to the nearest naira?
questions.explanation: Each payment accumulates for the time it is invested: 30,000(1.07)^4 + 40,000(1.07)^2 = 39,324 + 45,796 = N85,120. Option A accumulates both payments for 4 years, and option B forgets to accumulate the second payment at all. Option D uses simple interest for both.

questions.topic: Time Value of Money: Compound Interest and Discounting
questions.question: A payment of N50,000 is due at the end of year 1 and N70,000 at the end of year 5. At an effective rate of interest of 8% per annum, what single payment at the end of year 3 is equivalent to the two payments, to the nearest naira?
questions.explanation: At the comparison date of time 3, the earlier payment is accumulated 2 years and the later one discounted 2 years: 50,000(1.08)^2 + 70,000(1.08)^-2 = 58,320 + 60,014 = N118,334. Option C accumulates both payments, option B discounts both, and option A ignores interest altogether.

questions.topic: Time Value of Money: Compound Interest and Discounting
questions.question: An investor deposits N100,000 now and another N100,000 one year from now. At the end of year 2 the account holds N231,000. What effective annual rate of compound interest was earned?
questions.explanation: The equation of value at time 2 is 100,000(1 + i)^2 + 100,000(1 + i) = 231,000, i.e. x^2 + x - 2.31 = 0 with x = 1 + i, giving x = 1.1 and i = 10.00%. Option A divides the total interest of N31,000 by N200,000, ignoring timing. Option D halves that figure, and option B wrongly assumes the full N200,000 was invested for both years.

questions.topic: Time Value of Money: Compound Interest and Discounting
questions.question: Using an effective rate of interest of 6% per annum, what single payment at the end of year 4 is equivalent to N100,000 paid now and N100,000 paid at the end of year 2, to the nearest naira?
questions.explanation: The equivalent payment equals the accumulated value at time 4: 100,000(1.06)^4 + 100,000(1.06)^2 = 126,248 + 112,360 = N238,608. Option B accumulates both payments for 4 years, option A does not accumulate the second payment, and option C uses simple interest.

questions.topic: Time Value of Money: Compound Interest and Discounting
questions.question: Payments of N200,000 are due at the end of year 1 and at the end of year 2. At a nominal rate of interest of 10% per annum convertible half-yearly, what is their total present value, to the nearest naira?
questions.explanation: The half-yearly rate is 5%, so year 1 is 2 periods and year 2 is 4 periods: PV = 200,000(1.05)^-2 + 200,000(1.05)^-4 = N345,946. Option A treats 10% as an effective annual rate. Option C uses 1 and 2 half-years instead of 2 and 4, and option B discounts both payments for 2 years.

questions.topic: Time Value of Money: Compound Interest and Discounting
questions.question: A loan of N500,000 is to be repaid by two equal payments at the end of year 1 and the end of year 2, at an effective rate of interest of 10% per annum. What is each payment (to 2 decimal places)?
questions.explanation: The equation of value at time 0 is X(v + v^2) = 500,000 with v = 1/1.1, so X = 500,000/(0.909091 + 0.826446) = N288,095.24. Option B accumulates half the loan for one year, and option C accumulates the whole loan for 2 years and halves it, both ignoring that the payments are made at different times. Option D ignores interest.

questions.topic: Time Value of Money: Compound Interest and Discounting
questions.question: N100,000 is invested for 6 months at 20% per annum. Compare simple interest with compound interest (effective 20% per annum). Which statement is correct (to 2 decimal places)?

options.a: Compound interest gives N455.49 more than simple interest
options.b: Both give the same amount, N110,000.00
options.c: Compound interest gives N500.00 more than simple interest
options.d: Simple interest gives N455.49 more than compound interest

questions.explanation: For a period shorter than one year, simple interest gives more: 100,000(1 + 0.2 x 0.5) = N110,000.00 while 100,000(1.2)^0.5 = N109,544.51, a difference of N455.49. Option A reverses the direction; compound interest only overtakes simple interest after one full period. Option B is wrong because the two methods agree only at exactly one period.

questions.topic: Time Value of Money: Compound Interest and Discounting
questions.question: N80,000 grows to N100,000 in 2 years with interest compounded quarterly. What nominal rate of interest per annum convertible quarterly, i^(4), was earned (to 2 decimal places)?
questions.explanation: There are 8 quarters, so (1 + i^(4)/4)^8 = 1.25, giving i^(4)/4 = (1.25)^(1/8) - 1 = 2.83% and i^(4) = 11.31%. Option B is the effective annual rate (1.25)^(1/2) - 1, not the nominal quarterly rate. Option A is a simple-interest average, and option C is the quarterly rate that has not been multiplied by 4.

questions.topic: Present and Accumulated Values of Payment Streams
questions.question: An amount of N100 is invested now and accumulated for ten years at an effective rate of interest of 5% p.a. for the first three years, 6% p.a. effective for the next three years, and 7% p.a. effective for the remaining four years. Calculate the accumulated amount at the end of the ten-year period. (2 decimal places.)
questions.explanation: Accumulate each period in turn: 100 x 1.05^3 x 1.06^3 x 1.07^4 = 100 x 1.157625 x 1.191016 x 1.310796 = N180.73. Option A (N168.90) applies 7% for only three years instead of four, and options C and D wrongly use a single rate (7% or 6%) for all ten years.

questions.topic: Present and Accumulated Values of Payment Streams
questions.question: Which statement correctly describes the payments from a zero-coupon bond?

options.a: Regular coupons that rise and fall with an inflation index
options.b: Regular fixed coupons plus a redemption payment
options.c: No payment is ever made to the holder
options.d: A single payment at maturity whose money amount is known in advance

questions.explanation: A zero-coupon bond pays no coupons at all; the investor buys it at a price below face value and receives one known payment at maturity. Option B describes a fixed-interest security that pays coupons, and option A describes an index-linked security whose payments are not known in advance.

questions.topic: Present and Accumulated Values of Payment Streams
questions.question: For a fixed-interest security (ignoring the risk of default), are the money amounts of the coupon and redemption payments known in advance?

options.a: Yes, the amounts and dates are fixed at issue
options.b: No, they depend on an inflation index
options.c: Only the first coupon is known in advance
options.d: No, they depend on the issuer's profits each year

questions.explanation: A fixed-interest security pays coupons at a stated rate and a stated redemption amount on stated dates, so the cash amounts are known from the start (provided the issuer does not default). Option B describes an index-linked security, and option D describes something closer to equity dividends, which vary with profits.

questions.topic: Present and Accumulated Values of Payment Streams
questions.question: For an index-linked security, are the absolute (money) amounts of the payments known in advance?

options.a: Yes, they are fixed at issue
options.b: Yes, but only for the redemption payment
options.c: No, because the security never makes any payments
options.d: No, because the payments are adjusted in line with an index such as inflation

questions.explanation: An index-linked security links its payments to an index, commonly an inflation index, so the money amounts depend on future index values that are not yet known. Option A is true of zero-coupon and fixed-interest securities, not index-linked ones, and the redemption payment is also index-linked, so option B is wrong.

questions.topic: Present and Accumulated Values of Payment Streams
questions.question: An investor purchased a three-year index-linked security on 1.1.2001. In return the investor received payments at the end of each year plus a final redemption amount on 1.1.2004, all increased in line with the index below, relative to its value on the purchase date (1.1.2001). Without inflation the payments would have been GBP 1,200 each year and GBP 21,000 on redemption. Index values: 1.1.2000 = 100; 1.1.2001 = 120; 1.1.2002 = 110; 1.1.2003 = 130; 1.1.2004 = 105. Calculate the annual payment actually received by the investor on 1.1.2002.
questions.explanation: Each payment is scaled by the index on the payment date divided by the index at purchase, so 1200 x 110/120 = GBP 1,100. Option B is the unadjusted payment, which ignores that the index fell from 120 to 110.

questions.topic: Present and Accumulated Values of Payment Streams
questions.question: An investor purchased a three-year index-linked security on 1.1.2001. In return the investor received payments at the end of each year plus a final redemption amount on 1.1.2004, all increased in line with the index below, relative to its value on the purchase date (1.1.2001). Without inflation the payments would have been GBP 1,200 each year and GBP 21,000 on redemption. Index values: 1.1.2000 = 100; 1.1.2001 = 120; 1.1.2002 = 110; 1.1.2003 = 130; 1.1.2004 = 105. Calculate the annual payment actually received by the investor on 1.1.2003.
questions.explanation: Scaling by the index gives 1200 x 130/120 = GBP 1,300, since the index rose from 120 at purchase to 130. Option A uses the 1.1.2002 index value, and option D ignores indexation altogether.

questions.topic: Present and Accumulated Values of Payment Streams
questions.question: An investor purchased a three-year index-linked security on 1.1.2001. In return the investor received payments at the end of each year plus a final redemption amount on 1.1.2004, all increased in line with the index below, relative to its value on the purchase date (1.1.2001). Without inflation the payments would have been GBP 1,200 each year and GBP 21,000 on redemption. Index values: 1.1.2000 = 100; 1.1.2001 = 120; 1.1.2002 = 110; 1.1.2003 = 130; 1.1.2004 = 105. Calculate the annual payment (excluding the redemption amount) actually received by the investor on 1.1.2004.
questions.explanation: The 1.1.2004 payment is 1200 x 105/120 = GBP 1,050, because the index has fallen to 105 compared with 120 at purchase. Option C ignores indexation, and option A uses the earlier index value of 130.

questions.topic: Present and Accumulated Values of Payment Streams
questions.question: An investor purchased a three-year index-linked security on 1.1.2001. In return the investor received payments at the end of each year plus a final redemption amount on 1.1.2004, all increased in line with the index below, relative to its value on the purchase date (1.1.2001). Without inflation the payments would have been GBP 1,200 each year and GBP 21,000 on redemption. Index values: 1.1.2000 = 100; 1.1.2001 = 120; 1.1.2002 = 110; 1.1.2003 = 130; 1.1.2004 = 105. Calculate the redemption amount actually received by the investor on 1.1.2004.
questions.explanation: The redemption amount is indexed the same way as the annual payments: 21000 x 105/120 = GBP 18,375. Option B ignores indexation, and option C adds the final annual payment of 1,050 to the redemption amount, which is the total received that day rather than the redemption alone.

questions.topic: Present and Accumulated Values of Payment Streams
questions.question: The table describes whether, for different financial securities, the absolute amount of payments and the timing of payments are known in advance, using letters A - J, each of which is 'yes', 'no' or 'sometimes'. Contract (amount known in advance? / timing known in advance?): Zero-coupon bond (A / J); Fixed-interest security (B / I); Index-linked security (C / H); Call deposit (D / G); Equity (E / F). For the zero-coupon bond, which best describes A (is the absolute amount of payments known in advance)?
questions.explanation: A zero-coupon bond makes a single payment of a stated amount at maturity, so the amount is known in advance. Option C would suit a security whose payments can change, which is not the case here.

questions.topic: Present and Accumulated Values of Payment Streams
questions.question: The table describes whether, for different financial securities, the absolute amount of payments and the timing of payments are known in advance, using letters A - J, each of which is 'yes', 'no' or 'sometimes'. Contract (amount known in advance? / timing known in advance?): Zero-coupon bond (A / J); Fixed-interest security (B / I); Index-linked security (C / H); Call deposit (D / G); Equity (E / F). For equity, which best describes E (is the absolute amount of payments known in advance)?
questions.explanation: Equity dividends are decided by the company each time, depending on its profits, so the amount is not known in advance. Option A fits bonds with fixed coupons, and option C overstates how much shareholders can rely on a set dividend.

questions.topic: Present and Accumulated Values of Payment Streams
questions.question: The table describes whether, for different financial securities, the absolute amount of payments and the timing of payments are known in advance, using letters A - J, each of which is 'yes', 'no' or 'sometimes'. Contract (amount known in advance? / timing known in advance?): Zero-coupon bond (A / J); Fixed-interest security (B / I); Index-linked security (C / H); Call deposit (D / G); Equity (E / F). For the fixed-interest security, which best describes B (is the absolute amount of payments known in advance)?
questions.explanation: A fixed-interest security pays coupons and a redemption amount that are stated in money terms when it is issued, so the amounts are known in advance. Option B fits an index-linked security, whose payments move with an index.

questions.topic: Present and Accumulated Values of Payment Streams
questions.question: The table describes whether, for different financial securities, the absolute amount of payments and the timing of payments are known in advance, using letters A - J, each of which is 'yes', 'no' or 'sometimes'. Contract (amount known in advance? / timing known in advance?): Zero-coupon bond (A / J); Fixed-interest security (B / I); Index-linked security (C / H); Call deposit (D / G); Equity (E / F). For the fixed-interest security, which best describes I (is the timing of payments known in advance)?
questions.explanation: Coupons on a fixed-interest security are paid on set dates and the redemption date is fixed, so the timing is known in advance. Option C would describe a contract where payment dates can vary, such as one the issuer can redeem early.

questions.topic: Present and Accumulated Values of Payment Streams
questions.question: In actuarial and UK usage, a fixed-interest bond is also referred to as (loan) ________
questions.explanation: Fixed-interest bonds are often called stocks or loan stocks, as in UK government gilt-edged stock, because the holder owns a slice of a loan that pays fixed coupons. Option A is a contract whose value depends on another asset, and option D is the payment itself, not the security.

questions.topic: Present and Accumulated Values of Payment Streams
questions.question: A Lagos landlord will receive rent of N20,000 at the end of year 1, N30,000 at the end of year 2 and N50,000 at the end of year 3. Using compound interest at an effective rate of 10% per annum, what is the present value of these receipts at time 0, to the nearest naira?
questions.explanation: The present value of a stream is the sum of each payment times v^t: 20,000(1.1)^-1 + 30,000(1.1)^-2 + 50,000(1.1)^-3 = N80,541. Option D is the accumulated value at time 3, not the value today. Option C discounts with simple interest (dividing by 1 + 0.1t), and option A wrongly discounts the whole N100,000 for 3 years.

questions.topic: Present and Accumulated Values of Payment Streams
questions.question: A trader deposits N10,000 now (time 0), N15,000 at time 2 years and N25,000 at time 3 years into an account earning compound interest at 8% per annum effective. What is the accumulated value of the account at time 4 years, to the nearest naira?
questions.explanation: Each deposit grows for the time left until year 4: 10,000(1.08)^4 + 15,000(1.08)^2 + 25,000(1.08)^1 = N58,101. Option B accumulates all N50,000 for the full 4 years, ignoring the later deposit dates. Option C uses each deposit's own time t as the exponent instead of 4 - t, and option A is the present value at time 0.

questions.topic: Present and Accumulated Values of Payment Streams
questions.question: A pension fund expects N60,000 at the end of year 2 and N80,000 at the end of year 5. At an effective rate of compound interest of 6% per annum, what is the present value of the two amounts, to the nearest naira?
questions.explanation: PV = 60,000v^2 + 80,000v^5 with v = 1/1.06, giving 53,400.50 + 59,781.85 = N113,180. Option D swaps the discount periods of the two amounts, option B discounts the total for 5 years, and option A uses simple-interest discounting.

questions.topic: Present and Accumulated Values of Payment Streams
questions.question: Payments of N40,000 each are due at times 1, 3 and 5 years. Using compound interest at 5% per annum effective, what is the value of the three payments at time 3 years, to the nearest naira?
questions.explanation: At time 3 the first payment is accumulated for 2 years, the second is taken at face value and the third is discounted for 2 years: 40,000(1.05)^2 + 40,000 + 40,000(1.05)^-2 = N120,381. Option B discounts the last payment for only 1 year, while options A and C are the values at time 0 and time 5.

questions.topic: Present and Accumulated Values of Payment Streams
questions.question: A school owner pays a supplier N25,000 now, N25,000 at the end of year 1, N30,000 at the end of year 2 and N45,000 at the end of year 4. At 12% per annum effective compound interest, what is the present value of all the payments, to the nearest naira?
questions.explanation: The payment now is not discounted, so PV = 25,000 + 25,000(1.12)^-1 + 30,000(1.12)^-2 + 45,000(1.12)^-4 = N99,836. Option A discounts every payment by one extra year, treating the first one as if it were due at time 1. Option D leaves out the payment made now, and option C simply adds the payments without discounting.

questions.topic: Present and Accumulated Values of Payment Streams
questions.question: Payments of N50,000 at the end of quarter 1, N50,000 at the end of quarter 2 and N100,000 at the end of quarter 4 are valued at a nominal rate of interest of 12% per annum convertible quarterly (i^(4) = 0.12). What is their present value, to the nearest naira?
questions.explanation: The rate per quarter is 0.12/4 = 3%, so PV = 50,000(1.03)^-1 + 50,000(1.03)^-2 + 100,000(1.03)^-4 = N184,522. Option D wrongly uses 12% per quarter, option A treats 12% as an effective annual rate, and option B divides 12% by 3 instead of 4.

questions.topic: Present and Accumulated Values of Payment Streams
questions.question: A company must pay N200,000 at the end of year 1 and N300,000 at the end of year 2. Interest is at a nominal rate of 8% per annum convertible half-yearly. What is the present value of the two payments, to the nearest naira?
questions.explanation: With 4% per half-year, year 1 is 2 half-years and year 2 is 4 half-years: 200,000(1.04)^-2 + 300,000(1.04)^-4 = N441,352. Option A treats 8% as effective annual, option B counts years instead of half-years, and option C attaches the discount factors to the wrong payments.

questions.topic: Present and Accumulated Values of Payment Streams
questions.question: Using a constant force of interest delta = 0.08 per annum (so that v^t = e^(-delta t)), find the present value of N100,000 due at time 1 year and N150,000 due at time 3 years, to the nearest naira.
questions.explanation: With a force of interest, PV = 100,000e^(-0.08) + 150,000e^(-0.24) = 92,311.63 + 117,994.17 = N210,306. Option D treats 8% as an effective annual rate; with delta = 0.08 the effective rate is e^0.08 - 1 = 8.33%, so the correct discounting is slightly heavier and the true PV is lower. Option C accumulates instead of discounting, and option A discounts the total for 3 years.

questions.topic: Present and Accumulated Values of Payment Streams
questions.question: An investment pays N50,000 at the end of each year for 4 years. At an effective rate of compound interest of 10% per annum, what is its present value, to the nearest naira?
questions.explanation: The PV is 50,000(v + v^2 + v^3 + v^4) = 50,000 x a_4| = 50,000 x 3.1699 = N158,493. Option A treats the payments as made at the start of each year (annuity-due), option D is the accumulated value at time 4, and option B discounts the total of N200,000 for 4 years.

questions.topic: Present and Accumulated Values of Payment Streams
questions.question: A student saves N20,000 at the START of each year for 3 years (times 0, 1 and 2) in an account paying 7% per annum effective compound interest. How much is in the account at the end of year 3 (time 3), to the nearest naira?
questions.explanation: The deposits earn interest for 3, 2 and 1 years: 20,000[(1.07)^3 + (1.07)^2 + (1.07)] = N68,799. Option C assumes the deposits are made at the end of each year, so the last one earns no interest. Option D accumulates all N60,000 for 3 years, and option B applies simple interest to the total.

questions.topic: Present and Accumulated Values of Payment Streams
questions.question: An artisan deposits N12,000 at the end of every year for 5 years into a cooperative fund earning compound interest at 6% per annum effective. What is the accumulated value at the time of the 5th deposit, to the nearest naira?
questions.explanation: The accumulated value is 12,000 x s_5| = 12,000[(1.06)^5 - 1]/0.06 = 12,000 x 5.6371 = N67,645. Option D treats the deposits as made at the start of each year (one extra year of interest each), option A accumulates the total for 5 years, and option C is the present value.

questions.topic: Present and Accumulated Values of Payment Streams
questions.question: At 9% per annum effective, a_4| = 3.2397 and s_4| = 4.5731. What is the present value of N40,000 payable at the end of each year for 4 years, to the nearest naira?
questions.explanation: For level payments P in arrears, PV = P x a_4| = 40,000 x 3.2397 = N129,588. Option B uses s_4|, which gives the accumulated value at time 4. Option D multiplies by (1.09), which would value payments made at the start of each year, and option A discounts the total for only one year.

questions.topic: Present and Accumulated Values of Payment Streams
questions.question: A borrower owes N100,000 due at time 2 years and N150,000 due at time 5 years. The lender agrees to accept one payment at time 3 years instead. Using compound interest at 8% per annum effective, what single payment at time 3 is equivalent, to the nearest naira?
questions.explanation: Valuing both debts at time 3: 100,000(1.08)^1 + 150,000(1.08)^-2 = 108,000 + 128,600.82 = N236,601. Option C moves each debt in the wrong direction (discounting the earlier one and accumulating the later one). Option B ignores interest, and option A is the value of the debts at time 0, not time 3.

questions.topic: Present and Accumulated Values of Payment Streams
questions.question: A loan of N500,000 is repaid by N200,000 at the end of year 1, N200,000 at the end of year 2 and a final payment X at the end of year 3. Interest is at 10% per annum effective. Find X to the nearest naira.
questions.explanation: The equation of value at time 0 is 500,000 = 200,000v + 200,000v^2 + Xv^3, so X = (500,000 - 181,818.18 - 165,289.26)(1.1)^3 = N203,500. Option B is the outstanding present value but forgets to accumulate it to time 3. Option A ignores interest altogether, and option D accumulates the loan but subtracts the repayments without interest.

questions.topic: Present and Accumulated Values of Payment Streams
questions.question: Two debts of N50,000 each are due at times 2 years and 6 years. They are to be replaced by one payment of N100,000 at time t years. Using compound interest at 8% per annum effective, find t to 2 decimal places.
questions.explanation: The equation of value is 100,000v^t = 50,000v^2 + 50,000v^6 = 74,375.42, so t = ln(100,000/74,375.42)/ln(1.08) = 3.85 years. Option D is the simple average of the two dates, which is close but not exact under compound interest. Option A divides by 0.08 instead of ln(1.08), and option B mixes a base-10 logarithm on top with a natural logarithm underneath.

questions.topic: Present and Accumulated Values of Payment Streams
questions.question: A Lagos bakery is considering an oven costing N1,000,000 now. It is expected to generate net cash inflows of N400,000 at the end of each of the next 3 years. Using a discount rate of 12% per annum effective, what is the net present value of the project, to the nearest naira?
questions.explanation: NPV = PV of inflows - PV of outflows = 400,000(v + v^2 + v^3) - 1,000,000 = 960,732.69 - 1,000,000 = -N39,267. Option D ignores discounting and wrongly suggests a profit, option C has the sign reversed, and option A discounts the initial cost even though it is paid now.

questions.topic: Present and Accumulated Values of Payment Streams
questions.question: A poultry project requires N300,000 now and a further N100,000 at the end of year 1. It returns N250,000 at the end of year 2 and N300,000 at the end of year 3. At 10% per annum effective, what is the net present value, to the nearest naira?
questions.explanation: NPV = -300,000 - 100,000(1.1)^-1 + 250,000(1.1)^-2 + 300,000(1.1)^-3 = N41,097. Option A forgets the second outlay at year 1, option C treats that outlay as an inflow, and option D adds the cash flows without discounting.

questions.topic: Present and Accumulated Values of Payment Streams
questions.question: An investor in Ibadan can buy a business for N2,000,000 now. It will produce N800,000 at the end of year 1, N900,000 at the end of year 2 and N700,000 at the end of year 3. Her required return is 15% per annum effective. Based on NPV, what should she conclude?

options.a: NPV is about -N163,557; accept, as NPV is close to zero
options.b: NPV is about N400,000; accept, as inflows exceed the cost
options.c: NPV is about N182,918; accept, as NPV is positive
options.d: NPV is about -N163,557; reject, as it earns less than 15%

questions.explanation: NPV at 15% = -2,000,000 + 800,000(1.15)^-1 + 900,000(1.15)^-2 + 700,000(1.15)^-3 = -N163,557, which is negative, so the business returns less than 15% and should be rejected. Option B ignores discounting, option C discounts at 5% instead of the required 15%, and option A gets the right figure but the wrong decision.

questions.topic: Present and Accumulated Values of Payment Streams
questions.question: An investor pays N100,000 now and receives N55,000 at the end of year 1 and N60,500 at the end of year 2. At which effective annual rate of compound interest is the net present value of this transaction exactly zero?
questions.explanation: At 10%, 55,000/1.1 = 50,000 and 60,500/(1.1)^2 = 50,000, so the inflows are worth exactly N100,000 and the NPV is zero; this rate is the internal rate of return. Option C is the total gain of N15,500 as a percentage of the outlay, ignoring timing, and option A spreads that gain evenly over 2 years. At 12% (option D) the inflows are worth less than N100,000, so the NPV is negative.

questions.topic: Present and Accumulated Values of Payment Streams
questions.question: A project costs N100,000 now and returns N60,000 at the end of each of years 1 and 2. Setting the NPV to zero gives 60,000v^2 + 60,000v - 100,000 = 0. What is the internal rate of return (effective per annum), to 2 decimal places?
questions.explanation: Solving the quadratic gives v = 0.88444, so i = 1/v - 1 = 13.07%. Option C is the undiscounted gain of N20,000 as a percentage of the cost, and option B spreads that gain over 2 years; both ignore the timing of the payments. Option A treats the whole N120,000 as received at the end of year 2.

questions.topic: Present and Accumulated Values of Payment Streams
questions.question: At 10% per annum effective compound interest, compare Stream A (N60,000 at the end of year 1 and N60,000 at the end of year 3) with Stream B (N122,000 at the end of year 2). Which statement is correct?

options.a: A is worth more, since its first payment comes a year sooner
options.b: A is worth more by about N1,202 in present value
options.c: They are of equal value, since both are centred on year 2
options.d: B is worth more by about N1,202 in present value

questions.explanation: PV(A) = 60,000(1.1)^-1 + 60,000(1.1)^-3 = N99,624 and PV(B) = 122,000(1.1)^-2 = N100,826, so B is worth N1,202 more. Option A looks only at the first payment date instead of valuing all the payments, option B has the right gap but the wrong stream, and option C assumes payments placed symmetrically around a date are worth the same as one payment at that date, which is not true under compound interest.

questions.topic: Present and Accumulated Values of Payment Streams
questions.question: Option A pays N100,000 at the end of year 1. Option B pays N120,000 at the end of year 3. Using compound interest, which option has the higher present value at 5% per annum effective, and which at 12% per annum effective?
questions.explanation: At 5%, PV(A) = N95,238 and PV(B) = N103,661, so B wins; at 12%, PV(A) = N89,286 and PV(B) = N85,414, so A wins. A higher rate penalises the later, larger payment more heavily, so the preference switches. Option B ignores the effect of the higher rate, and option D reverses the effect.

questions.topic: Present and Accumulated Values of Payment Streams
questions.question: Payments of N100,000 are due at the end of each of years 1, 2 and 3. By how much does their present value FALL when the effective annual rate of compound interest rises from 5% to 10%, to the nearest naira?
questions.explanation: PV at 5% = N272,325 and PV at 10% = N248,685, so the PV falls by N23,640. Option B looks only at the first payment, option D discounts the total as if it were all due at year 3, and option C is the rise in accumulated value at time 3, which moves the other way.

questions.topic: Present and Accumulated Values of Payment Streams
questions.question: N50,000 is invested now and a further N50,000 two years from now. The account earns 6% per annum effective for the first 2 years and 8% per annum effective after that. What is the total accumulated at the end of year 6, to the nearest naira?
questions.explanation: The first deposit grows to 50,000(1.06)^2 by year 2, the second deposit joins it, and the total grows at 8% for 4 years: (50,000(1.06)^2 + 50,000)(1.08)^4 = N144,457. Option B applies the two rates in the wrong order, option C accumulates both deposits from time 0, and option D uses 8% for the whole period.

questions.topic: Present and Accumulated Values of Payment Streams
questions.question: Interest is 8% per annum effective during year 1 and 10% per annum effective during year 2. What is the present value at time 0 of N100,000 due at the end of year 1 and N100,000 due at the end of year 2, to the nearest naira?
questions.explanation: The year-2 payment is discounted through year 2 at 10% and through year 1 at 8%: 100,000/1.08 + 100,000/(1.08 x 1.10) = N176,768. Option B uses 10% for both years of the second payment, option A uses 8% throughout, and option D discounts the first payment at the year-2 rate.

questions.topic: Present and Accumulated Values of Payment Streams
questions.question: Tunde deposits N100,000 now and withdraws N30,000 at the end of year 2. The account earns 9% per annum effective compound interest. What is the balance at the end of year 4, to the nearest naira?
questions.explanation: Balance at year 4 = 100,000(1.09)^4 - 30,000(1.09)^2 = N105,515, because the withdrawn money would have earned interest for 2 more years. Option D acts as if the withdrawal happened at time 0, option A ignores the interest lost on the withdrawal, and option B discounts the withdrawal instead of accumulating it.

questions.topic: Present and Accumulated Values of Payment Streams
questions.question: A firm wants N1,000,000 at the end of year 3 to replace a generator. It will make 3 equal deposits at the end of each year into an account earning 8% per annum effective. What is each deposit, to the nearest naira?
questions.explanation: The equation of value at time 3 is X s_3| = 1,000,000, with s_3| = (1.08)^2 + 1.08 + 1 = 3.2464, so X = N308,034. Option D ignores interest, option A is the deposit that would work if deposits were made at the start of each year, and option B wrongly spreads the present value of the target over 3 years.

questions.topic: Present and Accumulated Values of Payment Streams
questions.question: Amaka wants N500,000 at the end of year 4. She makes 4 equal deposits at the START of each year (times 0, 1, 2 and 3) into an account paying 6% per annum effective. What is each deposit, to the nearest naira?
questions.explanation: Each deposit earns 4, 3, 2 and 1 years of interest, so X[(1.06)^4 + (1.06)^3 + (1.06)^2 + 1.06] = 500,000, giving X = 500,000/4.6371 = N107,826. Option D assumes end-of-year deposits, which need a larger amount, option A ignores interest, and option B spreads the present value of the target.

questions.topic: Present and Accumulated Values of Payment Streams
